title: Season uncertainty 'challenging' for AFLW community
text:
The 2026 men's AFL season is still being contested and we already know when next year's grand final is set to be.

Compare that to the AFLW, where this season's decider was announced just before the start of round three, 13 weeks before the date.

Key dates for the men's season are announced well in advance, with possible season start dates, Gather Round weekend and the grand final for next year already known to fans.

This gives clubs and players heading on their off-season breaks clarity when planning for personnel to return to the club. One benefit of this is being able to time pre-season training in order to be in peak condition when the season begins in March.

Former AFLW player and senior coach Lauren Arnell says more certainty would allow clubs to plan their pre-season to get the best performance out of the playing group.

"It's challenging when you don't have absolute security on that because one week more or less in your preseason has a significant impact on all planning, not just high performance, but on what you can educate as a footy program as well," Arnell told ABC Sport.

More certainty around the fixture would allow teams to optimise their pre-season training. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

The AFLW grand final will be played on November 27, after a 12-round home and away season.

The AFLW grand-final announcement came at half time of the men's Wildcard final between Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs, which the league said was a deliberate decision to get more coverage of the announcement.

Despite this, the broadcast on Foxtel/Kayo did not mention the announcement in the half-time break.

Men's players have 196 days from the key dates announcement to March 17, the earliest proposed date for the 2027 season to begin, and 395 days until next year's season decider. At the time of writing there are still 23 days until the 2026 grand final.

In a statement from the AFL accompanying the release, CEO Andrew Dillon highlighted the need for fans and clubs to be informed ahead of time.

"We're really pleased to be able to provide fans and clubs with this clarity well ahead of the 2027 season," Dillon said.

The AFL announced the women's fixture on May 21 of this year, giving clubs 80 days' notice, less than half the time their male counterparts have to prepare for the season.

Many AFLW players are still working full-time jobs outside their football careers and Arnell says more certainty would benefit them as well.

"There are still players in the competition working day jobs, and so those players letting their employers know has become more and more challenging," she said.

Rebecca Miller, who plays for the Richmond Tigers AFLW side, says an earlier fixture would also allow the league more time to promote the competition to fans.

"There's been times we've gone to community camps early in preseason or we've done appearances at a men's game early in the season and people are like, 'When are you playing?' And you're like, 'I don't know. I don't have a draw' so you just feel a bit silly in that regard," Miller told ABC Sport.

The last three AFLW grand finals have been sold out at Princes Park. (Getty: Josh Chadwick/AFL Photos)

Most AFL fans will know that the men's grand final is typically held in the last week of September and occasionally, like in 2027, in the first weekend of October. The AFLW grand final is yet to have that level of certainty, having been held in March, April, November and December across nine editions.

"It probably just goes back to that preparation; if we know the grand final, when and where it is before the season starts, again that marketing and promotion piece can really ramp up and make sure that our centrepiece is well attended and well watched and get the attendance they deserve," Miller said.

Conversely, the NRL announced its 2026 men's and women's fixtures on November 14, 2025, which gave NRLW clubs 230 days to prepare for their season to launch and allowed fans time to plan which games they want to attend the following season.

"They [the NRL] have the draw out for the men's and the women's team so at Christmas I can talk to my family about which games they're gonna go to and plan for it months in advance," Miller said, "to be able to go into the Christmas period and know your draw and be able to set yourself as a player but also as a fan and a member".

Richmond Tigers fans in Darwin celebrating a comeback win in their round three Dreamtime match against Essendon. (Getty: Celina Whan)

NRLW matches this year have had an average attendance of 4,915 after seven rounds. Round three of AFLW had an average crowd of 4,806 fans, which includes five double-headers with men's matches. If you count only standalone matches the average attendance is 2,293 for matches that provided a crowd number.

Miller believes that more notice would not just allow more time for promotion, it could also give players more motivation during a long preseason.

"It's so exciting and it just makes it all real. You circle a few games in particular from an individual point of view because you like playing that opposition or you have some beef against that opposition," she said.

"Your family and your friends can decide 'I want to come down to this game, come to that game' so it just makes it all real in your mind and you know why you're training, you know what you're training for".

Arnell believes the announcement of key dates is important but the next steps should come around fixturing.

"I think a priority for AFLW needs to be that all teams play each other once and then you start to land on where your season begins in a calendar and where your grand final sits," she said.

title: Breaking: Bathla Group will meet its payroll obligations
text:
Embattled property developer Bathla Group looks set to meet its payroll deadline today as its future hangs in the balance.

The ABC has confirmed with two sources with direct knowledge of the negotiations that some funding has been secured to meet some of Bathla's payroll obligations today.

Meanwhile negotiations are continuing between the administrator and lenders over short-term funding.

The ABC understands some of the lenders are still working through a short-term funding package to keep the company going for the next few weeks, with legal teams drafting the terms of this package.

While the group isn't being shut down, its situation remains precarious.

The first formal meeting of creditors is scheduled for Friday at 11am.

title: As Animalia turns 40, its author reflects on its extraordinary success
text:
In 1986, Graeme Base was a 28-year-old illustrator who had published one picture book, My Grandma Lived in Gooligulch, and was about to publish another.

His sophomore effort was an alliterative alphabet book lavishly illustrated in his baroque style, titled Animalia.

Whether the world needed another A-B-C book was debatable, but his publisher, Bob Sessions, was willing to take a punt.

The first hint of the phenomenal success the book would garner — coming in at number five on the New York Times list of the bestselling books of 1987 — was the response to an exhibition of the artwork held in the lead up to the book's publication.

Every piece — bar the two Base held onto (his favourites, Lazy Lions and Horribly Hairy Hogs) — sold before opening night.

"If I thought about it for 15 seconds, I probably wouldn't have started it," Base says of Animalia. (Supplied: Penguin)

It was a life-changing moment for Base and his wife, Robyn.

"Suddenly we had this little pot of money," Base says.

" We didn't invest it or put a deposit on a house — we bought two round-the-world air tickets and shot through for a year. "

They were backpacking through India and Nepal when Animalia came out, and received updates on the road.

"We were getting telegrams — that shows how long ago this was — from Bob saying 'we've reprinted again'," Base says.

The initial standard print run of 5,000 was doubled to 10,000, making the book a success from the outset.

"Three weeks later, they did another 10,000, then another 10,000, then another 10,000," Base says.

"Then they stopped mucking about and did 25,000. And then while we were away, we got news that they had just reprinted 50,000."

ABC Radio National’s Top 100 Australian Books Countdown We take over Radio National on Saturday, 17 and Sunday, 18 October to count down the Top 100 Australian books as voted by you.

Animalia has enjoyed unflagging popularity since it was first published four decades ago, with anniversary editions reprinted in 1996 and 2012.

It has sold more than 5 million copies worldwide and, earlier in 2026, was voted fifth in Guardian Australia's poll of Australia's best children's picture books.

In 2026, the book is being celebrated again, with the release of the Animalia: 40th Anniversary Edition and an Animalia Colouring Book.

A lucky break

Born in the UK, Base came to Australia when he was eight.

In England, Base had been a cocky and confident kid — "one of the lads", he says.

"When I got to Australia, I was anything but … I was this new kid in a tough Australian primary school with a very strong English accent who didn't know any of the schoolyard games.

"Any kid who finds himself in that position probably starts trying to figure out if they're good at something, start doing it to carve your niche in the playground and to make friends."

For Base, that was drawing.

Base dreamed of becoming an artist from the age of 11. (Supplied)

After graduating from graphic design at university, Base followed his classmates into advertising, which he soon realised was not the industry for him.

"I lasted maybe 18 months, went through three jobs, got fired from the third one," he says.

All the while, art remained his passion. He used his last pay cheque to print of some of his best illustrations, which he showed to publishers in the hope of finding work creating book jackets.

The work trickled in and after illustrating a couple of picture books, Base decided he could try his hand at writing one himself.

The result was My Grandma Lived in Gooligulch, published in 1981.

When Base showed Sessions the first completed pages — Crafty Crimson Cats and the Horrible Hairy Hogs — of his next book, the publisher was enthusiastic.

Base developed an interest in typography while studying graphic design at Swinburne University. (Supplied: Penguin )

Sessions took the finished pages to the high-profile Bologna Book Fair, where they caught the attention of publisher and editor Paul Gottlieb, who agreed to publish it in the US.

Base says it took him three years to finish the book, because he "was trying to be a rock star at the same time".

Still in his 20s, Base was leading a "double life", working on his children's book by day and playing in a rock band — named Rikitikitavi in a nod to Rudyard Kipling — at night.

The real drawcard, however, was the lead singer, Robyn, who Base, of course, ended up marrying.

The pair recently celebrated their 45th wedding anniversary — "a happy story," Base says.

From the US to China

What sent Animalia into the stratosphere was its unprecedented success in America.

Upon its US publication, the Bases, still on their round-the-world adventure, detoured to New York to do publicity for the book.

Base's first interview was a big one, with Charlie Gibson on Good Morning America — one of the country's most popular TV anchors on one of the highest rating shows.

When the cameras started rolling, Base responded to Gibson's warm welcome with a laconic "g'day".

The TV host was immediately charmed. "We just started riffing," Base says.

In his inexperience, Base forgot all about mentioning his new book — the reason he was there — which was sitting untouched on the coffee table.

Among Bases's favourite fellow Australian authors and illustrators are Bob Graham, Robert Ingpen and Shaun Tan. "He's the real deal," Base says. (Supplied: Penguin)

Fortunately, Gibson was more on the ball.

"With 30 seconds to go … he picked up the book off the coffee table and he held it to camera and did a hard sell that I couldn't have done to save my life — one of those, 'If you buy one book for your kids this Christmas, it's this one'."

The effect was dramatic.

"The book just flew off the shelves. Bookstores were caught unawares," Base says.

"The publishers went back to press and managed to catch the wave, and that year Animalia was the fifth biggest-selling book on the New York Times bestseller list."

For Base, it was a vindication of his youthful impetuosity.

"If we hadn't been stupid and bought around-the-world tickets we wouldn't have got ourselves to New York … [and] I wouldn't have done that interview," he says.

"[It's one of] those amazing things that do happen in life."

August's best books This month's best books include the latest from bestselling author Liane Moriarty, a debut novel set in 1920s Berlin and a tale of a mysterious Wyoming ghost town.

The success of Animalia kicked off a successful 30-year publishing career in the US, a rare feat for an Australian author.

While he says his "star has largely set in America", he has since found a growing market in China, after a trip to the Beijing Book Fair in 2017 led to a publisher picking up The Waterhole, a counting book full of elephants, giraffes and zebras.

The book "caught fire" and was added to a government-issued recommended reading list for schools.

"Every primary school in China finished up with multiple copies of The Waterhole, and it set off an interest in my work there," Base says.

Today, more than 20 of Base's books have been published in China, including Moonfish, a 2019 picture book inspired by a trip he took to Wuhan.

The Eleventh Hour

After the success of Animalia, Base faced a fresh challenge: how to write another book just as popular.

"The well-known term 'one-hit wonder' had a terrifying sort of resonance for me," he says.

An alphabet book offered limited scope for a sequel, so Base was compelled to come up with a new idea.

He'd read a few Agatha Christie novels during his travels and wondered if he could write a whodunnit for kids, where the clues were in the artwork rather than the text.

"I started working on that concept and almost immediately, the title, The Eleventh Hour, fell out of the air — I thought that's a great title for a mystery story," he says.

" I knew my story had to be centred around the number 11: 11 guests, an 11th birthday party, and at 11 o'clock something happens. "

It took some time to work out just what that something was. Initially, Base envisaged the victim as a dog, depicted slumped dead in a chair, killed by poison.

After Sessions gently pointed out that a picture book was not the place for a dead dog, Base went back to the drawing board.

He toyed with the idea of a jewellery heist but settled on a more kid-friendly crime: the theft of the party food.

It was up to readers of The Eleventh Hour to find out who stole the party food by deciphering clues hidden in the text. (Supplied: Penguin)

The Eleventh Hour was published in 1989 and became another global bestseller.

It was the joint winner (with Allan Baillie and Jane Tanner for Drac and the Gremlin) of CBCA's Picture Book of the Year.

Base believes his books are so popular with kids because he treats them "like grown-ups".

"I don't talk down to any perceived audience," he says.

"If there's a word in Animalia that they don't know or understand, well, you can look it up. That's what a dictionary's for.

"I'm not being arrogant about that. I think that's part of the fun of learning and discovery."

The sophisticated language of Animalia's V page — Victor V Vulture, the vaudeville ventriloquist, versatile virtuoso of vociferous verbosity, vexatiously vocalising at the Valhalla Variety Venue — did elicit a raised eyebrow from Sessions.

"Bob did say when I came to him with that one, 'Gee, that's pretty tough, isn't it?'" Base recalls.

"I said, 'Yeah, it is, but that's OK — I didn't know what vociferous meant until I looked it up. Surely kids can do the same."

Winners of the 2026 CBCA Awards A bittersweet story about a tree that becomes a pencil is one of the winners at Australia's top children's book awards.

Sessions was persuaded and the text stayed as it was — a decision Base believes would never be made today.

"I don't think there is a snowflake in hell's chance that that would have got through a committee without being simplified in this day and age," he says.

"These days, it's a lot more complicated. There are all sorts of reviews and anonymous readers and sales and marketing and cover committees … who will all put in their 20 cents worth, and you finish up with this thing which is trying to please too many masters."

He says he's never had any complaints from kids that his books are too hard.

"You're so much better off with kids not to put your hands on your knees and talk down to them, but to aim over their heads and challenge them to rise to the occasion," he says.

"And they will."

Animalia: 40th Anniversary Edition and an Animalia Colouring Book are published by Penguin Random House Australia.

title: Sydney Uni challenges $80k council fee for $5.6m kitchen renovation
text:
A university's refusal to pay an affordable housing charge to council while it undergoes a multi-million-dollar renovation has been escalated to the NSW government.

The University of Sydney (USYD) has sought approval of its $5.6 million proposal for the construction of a new kitchen to accommodate 100 students and "alterations and additions" to its Abercrombie student accommodation building in Darlington.

The City of Sydney Council had supported the development application on the condition USYD pay an $80,470 affordable housing contribution fee.

All development applications in the City of Sydney local area are required to make a contribution towards affordable housing.

The university says the redevelopment would renew and improve existing student accommodation at Abercrombie. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

The university has refused, arguing the development would renew and improve existing student accommodation, rather than add new beds.

At Wednesday night's council meeting, USYD's chief university infrastructure officer Debbie McNamara asked the local planning panel to consider removing the condition "due to the unique circumstances of the proposal".

"It is currently a 200-bed facility and will remain that … it does not increase current residential capacity," Ms McNamara said of the redevelopment.

The university says paying the charge would have "unintended consequences on the university's accommodation". (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

She argued that plans to increase the building's floor space for a new kitchen on ground level to 238 square metres had "automatically triggered" the charge.

She said paying the fee would set a precedent and would have "unintended consequences on the university's accommodation".

"We ask for the application to be considered on merit," she said.

The panel referred the application to Planning Minister Paul Scully's office for a decision on whether the condition would be approved or removed.

The ABC contacted Mr Scully's office for comment.

Do you know more? If you have any information about the story, contact Miriah Davis.

Crown Land challenge

A spokesperson for the City of Sydney Council said it was uncommon for an affordable housing contribution to be challenged by an applicant, but the university was located on state-owned land.

Disputed conditions on a development on Crown Land are referred to the minister by the local planning panel when an agreement cannot be met, according to the spokesperson.

"Where the applicant is a Crown authority, conditions such as the imposition of the affordable housing contribution can only be imposed with the agreement of the applicant," the spokesperson said.

The application has been referred to Planning Minister Paul Scully's office. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

A USYD spokesperson said it remained committed to providing affordable student housing and reiterated the proposal would not create additional student beds or increase occupancy.

"The proposed works at Abercrombie student accommodation are focused on improving dining and communal facilities and the residential experience for existing residents in response to student feedback," a spokesperson said. "In this instance, our position is that the affordable housing contributions are not applicable as our proposal is directed at improving our existing Abercrombie student accommodation rather than creating additional housing supply."

USYD 'progressing accommodation projects'

Last October, USYD's deputy vice chancellor Annamarie Jagose announced plans were underway to create 2,000 affordable student beds over the next five years.

The spokesperson did not answer specific questions from the ABC on how many beds had been delivered so far, but said it was "progressing a number of accommodation projects through planning, design and approvals".

The university was also "investing in restoring and improving" its existing accommodation through the redevelopment of 38 Victorian terraces on Darlington Road.

"We're also working with purpose-built student accommodation providers to make additional places available to students while our longer-term development pipeline progresses," the spokesperson said.

International students trading their rights for a bed International students relying on education agents to study in Australia might be misled about the country's housing situation.

USYD offers not-for-profit student accommodation with rental rates differing depending on the type of accommodation, location and length of the occupancy agreement.

Generally rates are offered below private market value, with a studio at the Abercrombie priced between $515 per week on a 52-week contract and $542 on a 26-week contract.

Other buildings provided by the university include the Regiment Building and Darlington House in Darlington and the Queen Mary building in Camperdown.

"We remain committed to increasing affordable accommodation opportunities for students and will continue investing in projects that improve accommodation both now and into the future," the spokesperson for USYD said.

title: Victorian town left without childcare service for two years calls for help
text:
A Victorian council mayor is "outraged" at a lack of support to fix issues plaguing a local early years childcare facility, and is calling on the Victorian government to intervene.

Hopetoun, located about 400 kilometres north-west of Melbourne, has been without a childcare service for over two years, and Yarriambiack Shire Council says it could potentially be without one for another two years.

Hopetoun Uniting Early Learning closed in April 2024 after workforce shortages forced the provider, Uniting Vic Tas, to cease operations.

In 2025, Emerge Early Years stepped in to deliver both child care and kindergarten services from a council-owned building, with staff recruited to restart child care in 2026.

However, earlier this year the council-owned centre was forced to close after a burst water pipe caused severe structural damage.

"The community was on the brink of finally getting the [childcare] service back," Yarriambiack Shire Mayor Andrew McLean said.

"Then, through no fault of their own, the council-owned building was declared unsafe after extensive water damage, mould and structural deterioration were uncovered."

Floors inside the Hopetoun childcare service building were damaged. (Supplied: Yarriambiack Shire Council)

Council said engineering assessments had confirmed the site required extensive stabilisation works that could potentially keep it out of action for up to two years.

"They've suggested it's going to take something like 18 months for the ground to dry out underneath before any works could recommence there," Cr McLean said.

"At the moment, all the floorboards have been ripped up to allow it to dry, but even after the 18 months of drying and compaction again, it'll be another I think 24 weeks or something to actually finish the unit."

Relocation causes headaches

In the meantime, the kindergarten programs, separate to the childcare service, were temporarily relocated to the Hopetoun Senior Citizens building, but that displaced those who had been using that facility.

"This temporary solution comes at the expense of another valued community group and still does not provide a childcare service for local families," Cr McLean said.

"We have 27 children enrolled in kindergarten this year, strong enrolment projections for next year, and at least 15 families who had already expressed interest in childcare places before services were due to reopen.

"The demand is there and the need is undeniable."

He called the situation "completely unacceptable", accusing the state government of failing to properly support rural communities and calling on them to deliver a new integrated early years facility for Hopetoun.

He wants to see the development of a facility on the Hopetoun P-12 College site, or a demolition and rebuild on the damaged council-owned site, with joint funding from council's insurance money and government support.

"Frankly, I am outraged that a rural community can be left in this position," he said.

"It is unacceptable that our children, teachers and educators are expected to operate a kindergarten program from the Senior Citizens building for up to two years."

The Hopetoun facility could take up to two years to reopen. (Supplied: Yarriambiack Shire Council)

A council representative said they had been told by the Department of Education that there were no relocatable facilities available and that investment in an alternative solution was not currently under consideration.

A Department of Education spokesperson said it was supporting ongoing kindergarten delivery in Hopetoun, while Yarriambiack Shire Council undertakes repairs to its existing early years building.

"While responsibility for childcare funding and provision rests with the Commonwealth, we've already offered council options to ensure the temporary kinder has what it needs for quality early learning, including new play equipment, more outdoor shade and secure fencing," the spokesperson said.

Parents feel the impact

Cr McLean also feared the ongoing absence of child care could affect local workforce participation, employee retention and the long-term future of the community.

"When parents can't access child care, they can't participate fully in the workforce … Employers struggle to recruit and retain staff," he said.

"When substandard kindergarten facilities are on offer, young families begin looking elsewhere.

"The ripple effects from these situations are profound."

It is a problem Beulah resident Heather Sherwell knows all too well.

The town's childcare issues have caused her partner to reduce his work hours and increased the family's travel time.

She said when they could organise family child care, it took them 15 minutes in one direction to drop their daughter off, before another 20 minutes in the opposite direction to drop her son off at kindergarten.

Heather Sherwell says her partner, Nathan Coffey, has had to reduce his work hours. (Supplied: Heather Sherwell)

Ms Sherwell said there was a feeling of defeat amongst parents in the region given the ongoing childcare situation.

"From an early learning perspective, it's impacting our kids … The relationships that children have with other children, the impact that those lack of relationships have in just basic play education," she said.

" Having the lack of support in infrastructure, having the lack of support in programs being promised and not delivered, it's very disheartening. "

She said the community needed government assistance with the infrastructure, but support was also required to support early years staff.

Member for Mildura Jade Benham has backed calls for the state government to provide a solution, but said she had also been told by the Department of Education that "there is no relocatable building available and that a $2.5 million rebuild is not justified".

"We have a situation where our seniors are being displaced so that our children can access kindergarten, while there is still nowhere to accommodate the child care families are asking for," she said.

"That is robbing Peter to pay Paul, and it is not a sustainable solution."

title: Fagan lashes Kangaroos over 'unfair' comments after Clarkson axing
text:
A shocked Chris Fagan has labelled North Melbourne's public explanation of coach Alastair Clarkson's axing "unfair" and hopes his old friend was given a chance to act on any feedback before the rug was pulled.

Clarkson, who coached Hawthorn to four premierships in an era-defining stint from 2005 to 2021, arrived at North as head coach amid great fanfare after being appointed in August 2022.

Yesterday, with a year to run on his contract, he was unceremoniously axed by football boss Todd Viney, a close friend, and club president Sonja Hood.

Clarkson sacked as Kangaroos hunt 'coach for the modern game' North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney explain why the club is parting ways with Alastair Clarkson with a year to run on his deal.

Asked what type of coach the Kangaroos wanted, Hood, who declared Clarkson's appointment had not been an error, said: "This club needs a coach who can coach for the modern game.

"It'll be a coach who knows what they're doing, and it'll be a coach who's the best fit for this football club."

Viney said there were "still some gaping holes in our game plan" and Clarkson's efforts to fill them only led to "more meetings, more information and players … becoming a bit more confused".

The pair said a canvassing of the club, including players, revealed he no longer had the belief of enough people that he was the right coach to take the group forward.

"I hope he's okay," Brisbane Lions coach Fagan, who first worked with Clarkson at Melbourne in the late 90s before they joined forces at Hawthorn, said.

"I just hope that the feedback that was given at the press conference yesterday about him was given to him in person at some stage during this year, so that he had a chance to act on it.

" It was a pretty fierce press conference. The way that he was spoken about. I reckon probably an unfair description of the man that's done awful lot for footy. "

The 58-year-old's departure comes despite the Kangaroos's improved season in 2026, when they finished 14th and claimed nine wins.

"It was a big shock to me. I actually thought, 'That can't be right,'" Fagan said of the call.

"Under his guidance, North really started to improve. It just reminded me of how tough coaching can be.

"That when a bloke that's been as successful as him as a coach can be jettisoned as quickly as that."

Alastair Clarkson (left) and Chris Fagan were central figures in the investigation into racism at Hawthorn during their time at the club. (Getty Images: Adam Trafford/AFL Media)

The pair were central figures in Hawthorn's racism saga that was settled after two years of legal turmoil in 2024.

Clarkson took a mental health break in 2023 while Fagan, who has the Brisbane Lions in sight of a third-straight flag, admitted he came close to doing the same before opting to coach on.

Fagan, who has yet to speak to Clarkson, hopes his old mate is not lost to the game, and chuckled at the thought of him in a media role, given his typically frosty relationship with that industry.

"We go back a long way and we'll still be friends and still talk a lot about footy, and I'll still seek his advice, no doubt," Fagan said.

AAP

title: Current cricket schedule could hurt women's game, says Perry
text:
Ellyse Perry has called for Australia's women to be given regular cricket in the peak of summer, fearing the current schedule could stunt the game.

Australia will play nine white-ball matches at home this summer against Bangladesh and New Zealand, with all confined to October and March.

The Australian team has not played a game at home during the summer school holidays since January 2025, while the WBBL also now falls entirely during the school term.

Part of the issue for officials has been India's WPL moving to the January window, with a common fear it will eventually extend into most of February.

Australia's only home matches in the middle of summer under the current program, which runs until the end of 2029, are white-ball ones against Ireland in the first half of December 2028.

Ellyse Perry feels that the lack of cricket in the school holidays will hurt the women's team. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Australian players have long pushed for a regular spot in the summer, much like the Boxing Day Test in Melbourne and New Year's Test in Sydney are part of the national calendar.

"It's the best time of year to play across that school-holiday window," Perry said.

"People are at home, everyone's head is in cricket too. There is a lot on the schedule in both the men's and women's game. It's a nice time to go out and watch.

"But also for them to be inspired to play themselves and be involved in cricket, it's really important.

"I don't know what the perfect window is, but I think somewhere in the peak of the Australian summer is important to carve out.

"Where and how you do that is more of a strategic planning opportunity that will take some time to find. But we should be prioritising that for the Australian team."

None of the WBBL games are being played in the school holidays this summer. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

There is the view that being pushed to the outskirts of summer also has the potential to stunt any momentum around the team after its dominant T20 World Cup.

The timing of the WPL means the only real window during the school holidays would be in the second half of December, perhaps in the lead-up to Christmas.

"It's not just for Australia and all the southern-hemisphere countries … to make sure we're encouraging people to come along to matches," Perry said.

"It's a really tricky one; the scheduling and planning is a matrix I would never want to look at.

"But it would be really nice for us to preserve a window there where people know the Australian women's team is playing so they have the means and opportunity to come watch.

"That's really important in terms of continuing to grow the game for young boys and girls. But also we want to play in front of a home crowd with good opposition each year."

AAP

title: British-backed CPC buys another NT station for $47.4m
text:
Consolidated Pastoral Company (CPC) has continued to expand its vast portfolio of properties across Australia by buying Vermelha Station in the Northern Territory.

According to documents from the NT Land Titles Office, Vermelha was sold for $47.4 million in a deal understood to include about 15,000 head of cattle and a 2,956-megalitre a year water licence.

The 204,000-hectare station is located near the town of Larrimah, 500 kilometres south of Darwin, and had been owned by Vietnamese investors since 2016.

Owned by British billionaires Guy and Julia Hands, CPC has been on a spending spree over the last few years, acquiring a number of properties including the Beetaloo Aggregation in the Northern Territory for more than $300 million and Australia's largest sheep station Rawlinna in Western Australia.

According to CPC's website, the company's asset base now exceeds $1.7 billion and runs more than 400,000 head of cattle, 50,000 goats and 150,000 sheep "across more than 6 million hectares of land", plus feedlots in Indonesia.

Vermelha Station is near the town of Larrimah, NT. (ABC Rural: Sam Parry)

CPC becomes major water licence holder

CPC is one of Australia's largest cattle companies and is on track to be the Northern Territory's biggest irrigator.

Its acquisition of Vermelha Station and its 2,956ML water licence takes the company's overall groundwater licence holdings in the Northern Territory to 18,524ML per year, including:

Powell Creek — 480 ML/year

Dungowan — 4,738 ML/year

Newcastle Waters — 3,060 ML/year

Tandyidgee — 7,290 ML/year

Vermelha — 2,956ML/year

Speaking to ABC Rural in August, after receiving water licences for Powell Creek, Dungowan, Tandyidgee and Newcastle Waters, CPC chief executive Troy Setter said the plan was to use water to grow crops for cattle.

Loading...

"We've been dryland cropping on those [Barkly] stations for a couple of years now, growing sorghum, hay and also a bit of cotton when the market was right," he said.

"So the plan is to develop some of that farming land for irrigation.

" It will give us the opportunity to have more consistent cropping and consistent production which will flow to higher productivity [for our cattle operations]. "

Mr Setter said the irrigation developments would be done through a staged approach and he hoped the first pivots could be installed next year.

The water licence at Vermelha has been under-utilised, with water currently used for one 45-hectare pivot irrigator and 60 hectares of cleared land.

However the station does have a clearing permit for 3,659 hectares.

title: This abattoir wants to hire 60 people but just one Australian applied
text:
West Australian abattoirs and pork producers say recent visa changes and the near impossibility of attracting local employees to fill vacancies are leaving them facing severe worker shortages.

Just one Australian resident responded when an abattoir took out advertisements seeking 60 skilled workers for its facility near Broome in WA's far north Kimberley, according to Yougawalla Pastoral Company general manager Haydn Sale.

Mr Sale's company is helping reopen the abattoir after years of dormancy, but he said the opening date had been pushed back months due to staffing issues.

Meanwhile, the expansion of a piggery in the state's south will go ahead with a significantly reduced workforce for the same reasons.

New visa rules

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke issued a ministerial direction in July outlining a new five-tier visa processing hierarchy that strongly favoured applicants already located inside Australia.

The lowest priority was given to applicants based overseas seeking employment in industries unrelated to law enforcement, defence, construction, healthcare, and teaching.

Tony Burke has changed skilled worker visa processing priorities. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Sale said nearly 30 skilled workers from the Philippines had been identified to work at Pindan Beef Co, formerly the Kimberley Meat Company, located about 2,300 kilometres north of Perth, as had 13 of the workers' partners.

But he said the skilled worker visa changes had made a 2026 opening date impossible.

"We've had to move [that date] back … because the skilled meatworker visas that we've applied for are basically held up in the system," he said.

" We paid $390,000 in visa fees to get those people in, and now we're just in a holding pattern on that. "

Mr Sale said hiring locally was not an option due to a shortage of skilled Australian workers and the remoteness of the plant, with just a single Australian applicant for the 60 advertised positions.

"Upon investigation, they weren't even actually skilled," he said.

Haydn Sale says the abattoir cannot reopen until workers' visas have been processed. (Supplied: Haydn Sale)

The soft opening of the facility is now slated for February, with the full commercial opening delayed until April.

Mr Sale said thousands of cattle were in limbo waiting to be processed.

"We've got a whole supply chain that was lined up on the stations," he said.

" We had about 6,500 cattle ready to process through late in the year that we're now having to find homes for. "

Piggery staff challenges

In the south of the state, near Narrogin, pork producer Dawson Bradford is facing similar challenges while trying to expand his piggery from 1,500 to 2,500 sows.

Hillcroft Farms near Narrogin is expanding its facility. (Supplied: Dawson Bradford)

Mr Bradford said overseas workers were crucial to his 5,000-hectare mixed farming enterprise, forming 90 per cent of his piggery workforce and more than half of his total staff.

"We bring them in because they want to live in the bush and they want to work in the industry," he said.

"We just cannot get Australians who want to work through the piggery, and other industries are exactly the same, whether it's chickens, processing, abattoirs.

"We're all in the same boat. We're just relying on that migrant labour to come in, and they're skilled, they are good workers."

Workers under pressure

Mr Bradford said many of those he recruited in January were from the Philippines, and some had already left their previous employment, believing they would soon be in Australia.

"We don't know when they're going to get here," he said.

" We need them now. "

Regardless of when the workers' visas would be processed, Mr Bradford said the piggery expansion would proceed as plans were set in motion last year.

"That's when we got the ball rolling with getting stock and breeding them out to mate, so the piglets are due in six months," he said.

"They're coming and we won't have staff, so it's going to load up the rest of the staff … just because these visas are being held up."

Mr Bradford says the existing team at Hillcroft Farms will have to manage the expansion themselves. (Supplied: Dawson Bradford)

He said his attempts to gain clarity on when the visas he applied for might be processed had so far been futile.

"You cannot talk to anyone, you cannot get hold of anyone in that department to give you an update," he said.

"You just have no idea when your applications are going to be processed."

Government responds

A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said the skilled migrant program had been designed to put Australian workers first.

"Where Australian businesses have been unable to find local workers, the skilled migration system supports Australian businesses to access migrant workers with these skills, making a positive contribution to the economy," the spokesperson said.

"The department is continuing to process applications under Meat Industry Labour Agreements in accordance with program requirements and established processing arrangements."

title: Scurvy listed as most likely factor in 6yo Qld boy's death
text:
A coroner has found scurvy to be the "most likely underlying factor" in the death of a Queensland boy with Down syndrome.

Six-year-old Connor Dean died in the Queensland Children's Hospital on August 10, 2024, after his heart stopped following a general anaesthetic, and he experienced a severe brain injury from a lack of oxygen.

He weighed just 14.1kg when he died.

In non-inquest findings, Deputy Queensland Coroner Stephanie Gallagher, backed a forensic pathologist's opinion that Connor died from "hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy due to cardiac arrest following general anaesthetic, in the setting of vitamin C deficiency".

She found Down syndrome was a "contributing factor".

"Although the precise mechanism leading to the cardiac arrest could not be definitively determined, the treating clinicians and forensic pathologist considered vitamin C deficiency to be the most likely underlying factor," Ms Gallagher wrote.

Connor had surgery as a baby for a heart defect, was developmentally delayed and communicated using "mostly single words".

He walked and ran with a "wide-based gait".

About a month before his death, his parents reported he started walking with a "shuffling gait which progressed to limping" and eventually he refused to weight bear.

Scurvy a 'likely unifying diagnosis'

He was admitted to the Queensland Children's Hospital for investigation, which included a scan under general anaesthetic.

Connor went into cardiac arrest following the scan and was revived after 8-10 minutes of cardio-pulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

As his condition deteriorated and opinions were sought from various specialists, his family was told "severe life-threatening scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) seemed a likely unifying diagnosis".

His parents said they were unaware of their son's Vitamin C deficiency until after his cardiac arrest.

Connor's paediatrician, who had about 20 years' experience in the specialty, told Ms Gallagher in a statement he had "significant concerns regarding Connor's growth and nutritional deficiencies for a long time".

In November 2023, he said he discussed with Connor's mother that the boy's diet was inadequate to meet his vitamin and mineral requirements" but he believed his needs were being met with his intake of multivitamin supplements.

During Connor's admission just before his death, his mother advised he was taking a multivitamin and his immunisations were up to date.

Connor's paediatrician told the coroner he was concerned the product, which was not named in Ms Gallagher's findings, was available in Australia.

"I believe that it is misleading to call this product a multivitamin when it misses essential vitamins such as Vitamin C," the medical specialist said.

Given the absorption of plant-based iron is greatly enhanced by Vitamin C, he said it was "illogical" to have an iron-containing product in combination with multiple vitamins, but not Vitamin C.

"It is my clinical opinion that Connor would not have had Vitamin C deficiency, and the clinical features of scurvy that lead to his death, if he had been taking a different multivitamin that contained Vitamin C," the paediatrician said.

But the manufacturer of the multivitamin told Ms Gallagher in response: "Multivitamin products do not generally contain all essential vitamins and nor are they indicated for treatment of a severe deficiency.

"They are indicated to help supplement when dietary intake is inadequate."

The manufacturer told the coroner that given "the apparent lack of monitoring of Connor's Vitamin C deficiency prior to his arrest, there is no basis on which to draw the conclusion that" the multivitamin contributed to Connor's death.

"Any such uncertainty should not be resolved by the adoption of a single clinical opinion by a non-independent clinician in the circumstances," the manufacturer wrote.

Ms Gallagher did not address the multivitamin issue in her conclusions.

"The evidence establishes that Connor Dean had severe Vitamin C deficiency, with associated … features consistent with scurvy, and that he suffered a cardiac arrest following the administration of a general anaesthetic," she wrote.

"I extend my condolences to Connor's family and loved ones for their loss."

title: Zoo's baby chimpanzee to be sent away after mother's rejection
text:
A central Queensland zoo will send a baby chimpanzee elsewhere after a failed reunion with its mother.

Female chimp Sile gave birth to Cassie at the Rockhampton Zoo in June, but dropped the baby when it was hours old, breaking its leg.

Zookeepers then had to care for Cassie round the clock as they tried to mimic all interactions as closely as they could to typical chimpanzee behaviour.

Keepers have had to work around the clock caring for Cassie, trying to mimic interactions with chimp behaviour. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

After healing, staff attempted to re-introduce Cassie to mother Sile as well as another female adult in the troop, Mary.

But it was unsuccessful, with both females showing aggression towards Cassie, who was left with bruising and bite marks.

At the time the zoo said it would discuss possible next steps with experts in the field.

Cassie had positive reactions to the troop through mesh screens before the unsuccessful reunion. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

In a social media video posted on Thursday morning, primate team leader Jo Thrower said Cassie had healed well from the interactions.

"From this we've had a lot of discussions within our team and with specialists from around Australasia and Europe," Ms Thrower said.

"We've concluded that Cassie needs to find a new troop to go to and become a part of."

Ms Thrower said it was very important for the young chimp's development to be around others of its kind as soon as possible.

"Staying in human care she's going to grow up believing she's a human, which will only cause bigger issues down the line when she does eventually go in with chimps," she said.

"The sooner we can get this done the better."

She conceded that the Rockhampton community already "loved" Cassie and would like to see the chimp grow up locally.

"But we need to do what's best for her welfare, and to put her back in with our troop she's only going to get hurt."

Rockhampton Zoo curator Blair Chapman nursing baby Cassie, who is receiving 24/7 care from keepers. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Where to next?

Ms Thrower said Cassie's development was going well and the chimp was hitting all the appropriate milestones.

The zoo did not confirm which facility Cassie would be sent to as it was "still working through options" and would update the community as soon as the final decision was made.

Cassie is the offspring of 19-year-old alpha female Sile and the troop’s alpha male, Alon. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

The zoo is owned and funded by the Rockhampton Regional Council which has not yet responded to the ABC about the costs incurred with hand-rearing Cassie.

The young chimp was named after chimpanzee Cassius, a resident at the Rockhampton Zoo for almost 40 years, and a local woman named Cassie who donated colostrum during the initial weeks after the primate's birth.

Cassie will leave behind a seven-chimp troop with four males aged from six to 30 years old and three females aged between eight and 23.

title: Theft of sanitary items demonstrates period poverty desperation
text:
Using socks as sanitary pads, wearing tampons for more than two days and stealing products from supermarkets are just some of the lengths women and girls are going to in order to afford period products.

Cate Sherlock is an Adelaide-based social worker and says it is an invisible struggle plaguing communities across the state.

"Young women entering supermarkets and stealing products for the month is a recurring thing I hear," she said.

Cate Sherlock would like to see psycho-social assessments include period product affordability. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"They are wearing period products for a long period of time and then getting asked about their hygiene because they start to smell.

"There is stigma and shame about having poor self-care, when in reality they can't afford multiple period products in a day."

With 66 per cent of people who menstruate struggling to afford period products in SA at some point, many say the state needs to catch up and address its menstrual inequality issue.

Cate Sherlock says stealing is a recurring thing she hears from people experiencing period poverty. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Teachers paying out of pocket

The ABC heard from five government workers, including teachers, who were witnessing period poverty first-hand.

Three spoke under the condition of anonymity due to their roles in the public sector.

"I know the year 6 teachers buy products and leave them in the drawers in their classroom so girls can access them," one SA wellbeing teacher said.

One teacher says other education budgets were often utilised to purchase sanitary products. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"Many families are struggling to put food on the table.

"[They] are struggling to pay for such expensive products and it's going to get worse with our current climate."

A public high school teacher said social justice budgets were often utilised to purchase sanitary products.

Some teachers say they leave period products in drawers in their classroom so girls can access them. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"My site purchases supplies from our wellbeing budget so teachers don't feel they have to, [just] to ensure students have access to a range of products if they need them," the teacher said.

A public service social worker recounted how she has been having a conversation with someone about period poverty "close to once a fortnight".

"A lot of homeless women tell me they use items such as socks rather than sanitary pads and tampons due to the cost," she said.

" I recently had a [woman] fleeing domestic violence choose between putting petrol in their car over pads or tampons so they could flee in the middle of the night. "

SA, NT and Tasmania 'failing' people

Not-for-profit organisation Share the Dignity surveyed more than 150,000 Australians who menstruate in 2024.

Of those, 66 per cent of South Australians had struggled to afford period products at some point.

Chief executive Rochelle Courtenay said period poverty was a national issue that was growing, with the charity to date donating 6.2 million packets of period products since it began in 2015.

Rochelle Courtenay says 200,000 packets of period products are only enough to last 50,000 women for four months. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"When the data came out in 2024 we had 3.3 million Australians living below the poverty line," she said.

"That number has now increased to 5.5 million Australians."

Ms Courtenay said the only states and territories "failing" were Tasmania, the Northern Territory and South Australia.

"ACT is leading the way with a bill passed that makes it mandatory to provide period products in [places where] somebody is being educated, as well as hospitals, libraries and communal places," she said.

Some Australian states have period product vending machines. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"In Victoria, they have just rolled out 1,400 free period product vending machines, and they provide period products [in most public spaces].

"In Queensland, period products are in every primary and secondary school, as well as WA and New South Wales."

Legislative change needed

Former South Australian Legislative Council MP Connie Bonaros put forward the Period Products and Facilities (Access) Bill in March 2025.

The proposed bill was modelled on the ACT's which came into effect in 2023.

While the bill did not pass the Lower House and Ms Bonaros is no longer acting as a member of parliament, legislative change is still what she wants to see.

"We had the opportunity to lead the way when it comes to period poverty in South Australia, now we're playing catch up," she said.

Connie Bonaros says while SA had the opportunity to lead in change, it is now playing catch-up. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

The state government previously committed a total of $564,000 in 2023 over three years to fund free period products in some public schools.

It was an initiative Ms Bonaros said had likely only funded around 1,250 students with products.

"Victoria introduced its [period product] funding model and they threw $23 million towards a similar program rollout," she said.

Ms Bonaros said not-for-profit charities like Kickstart for Kids, of which she is an ambassador, donates more than 2,000 products a month to 200 SA public schools.

"Sadly we're a far cry from where we need to be," she said.

Teachers have purchased sanitary items out of their own pocket for their students. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Minister for Education Lucy Hood declined an interview, and a department spokesperson did not confirm whether legislative reforms would be considered in the future.

In a statement the department said it currently provided period products to more than 500 public schools.

"This program will continue in our schools, supporting around 50,000 students each year," the statement read.

"All South Australian public schools with year 5 and above enrolments receive funding to provide period products, with additional support directed to schools experiencing greater disadvantage."

It is a reality Connie Bonaros said needed to change.

title: Medvedev puts bird disruption aside to claim win at US Open
text:
Daniil Medvedev overcame an unusual interruption from two birds to fly into the third round of the US Open as he flattened American wildcard Sebastian Gorzny 6-1 6-3 7-5 at Louis Armstrong Stadium on Wednesday, local time.

The 2021 champion fired off 14 aces in a lopsided affair, where a mid-match avian distraction served up an odd bit of drama. Medvedev next plays either Spain's Jaume Munar or Frenchman Arthur Rinderknech.

"Being on the court, I was happy with my level," the Russian said.

"I love this court and I love you guys."

The Russian broke his opponent from the baseline in the opening game and needed only 21 minutes to get through the first set, firing off 10 winners to just two from Gorzny, who was outmatched in only his second major main draw match.

Medvedev has kept a calm demeanour in New York — in contrast to his dramatic first-round exit last year — but had his patience tested when a pair of birds appeared on the net during a rally midway through the second set, prompting the umpire to replay the point.

"I saw them straight away and thought the point would stop straight away," said Medvedev, who estimated that they continued to play for 45 seconds before the umpire intervened.

"The moment I hit the winner, we stop, and I say, 'Why?'"

Daniil Medvedev was unhappy that the umpire paused the game. (Reuters: Shannon Stapleton)

He got over it pretty quickly, keeping the demolition job going in the third set, where he briefly sniped at the chair umpire, calling him "crazy," during the changeover after the third game and survived a 33-shot rally in the sixth.

Gorzny improved his level in the third set, saving four break points in the ninth game, but it was too little too late as Medvedev harnessed his powerful forehand to break the American in the 11th game and sealed it with an unreturnable serve.

The bird incident joined a growing list of odd moments in Flushing Meadows for Medvedev, who has endured a love-hate relationship with the New York crowd since his memorable turn as pantomime villain in 2019.

He overcame a booing crowd to beat Spaniard Feliciano Lopez en route to the final that year, losing to Rafa Nadal in the championship match but earning the fans' begrudging respect.

"This would definitely be in the top five [unusual moments]," Medvedev told reporters.

"It's OK. It happens."

Reuters

title: LA Clippers fined $40m over 'flagrant' rules breaches
text:
The NBA has imposed a sweeping punishment against the Los Angeles Clippers for violating salary cap circumvention rules, suspending owner Steve Ballmer for one year, fining the team $US30 million ($41.5 million) and forcing it to forfeit five draft picks.

Two-time NBA Finals MVP Kawhi Leonard was also hit with a $US700,000 ($977,000) penalty, president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank was banned for six months and team president of business operations Gillian Zucker was suspended for one year.

The league came down hard on the organisation on Wednesday after a nearly year-long investigation led by an outside law firm.

The Clippers had said multiple times that they had done nothing wrong and expected to be exonerated.

"I think that we're going to be in the clear," Leonard said in April, "so I'm not stressing it."

At the same time, Frank said: "If you know Steve and know Steve's integrity, you know there's nothing to it. We believe and we've very confident we're on the right side of this."

The team maintained that stance on Wednesday.

Steve Ballmer (left) will sit out the next 12 months as part of his punishment for the breaches. (Getty Images: Katelyn Mulcahy)

"We vehemently reject the NBA's findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence," the team said in a statement.

"What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly, and they have not held themselves close to the standard Commissioner [Adam] Silver set at the start of this investigation to ensure its fairness and accuracy."

The Clippers said they will "now fight just as hard to demonstrate our innocence. We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process."

The league said it and the players' union agreed to confirm the penalties as final and binding on all parties. It said the outside law firm continued to receive information involving the investigation, and the league "will consider further action as appropriate".

"I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct," Silver said in a statement.

"The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations."

Adam Silver says he is "deeply disappointed" in the Clippers' breaches. (Getty Images: Elsa)

The NBA began investigating in September 2025 whether a $28 million endorsement contract between Leonard and Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC — a company that filed for bankruptcy last year — broke league rules, following a report by journalist Pablo Torre.

Earlier this year, Aspiration co-founder Joseph Sanberg was sentenced to 14 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to defrauding investors and lenders of at least $248 million.

The Clippers released a letter from Ballmer's attorney David Kelley to Silver, in which he described the investigation as "a witch hunt" and the subsequent penalties as a "gross injustice".

Kelley accused Silver of not keeping his promises that the investigation would be governed by due process and fundamental fairness, as well as the burden being on the league to prove any violations through evidence.

"League counsel has acknowledged in our discussions that the league does not believe there was an agreement between the Clippers and Aspiration to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard. League counsel also agreed with the Department of Justice, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and a federal judge that Mr. Ballmer was a victim of Joe Sanberg's fraud — not a participant," wrote Kelley, a partner in the firm O'Melveny and Myers.

"Mr Ballmer's reputation has been irreparably damaged as he now finds himself embroiled not only in this heavily biased investigation, but in civil litigation, the Aspiration bankruptcy proceeding, and more," Kelley wrote.

Kelley wrote that no league rule prohibits team personnel from making introductions to both sponsors and vendors in response to player requests.

"Retroactively punishing the Clippers for violating a rule that never existed is hardly consistent with due process," Kelley wrote.

The league said Ballmer knowingly sought to help Leonard obtain off-court income deals, approved a business deal that he knew was a precondition for Aspiration to enter into an endorsement contract with Leonard, and for failing to create conditions under which his team followed league rules.

"I accept full responsibility for lapses in judgement by people within my inner circle and regret the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family," Leonard said in a statement issued through his new agent, Harrison Gaines.

The NBA said Leonard, through his former business manager and uncle Dennis Robertson, "violated the circumvention rules by pressuring the Clippers to assist him in obtaining off-court income opportunities, successfully obtaining those opportunities, and failing to reimburse payments by the Clippers for personal expenses."

"I entered into my contract with the Clippers as well as the agreements in question in good faith, fully committed to fulfilling my obligations and with no knowledge of any intent on anyone's part to circumvent the salary cap," Leonard said in his statement.

The league said Ballmer was suspended for "knowingly seeking to help Mr Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities," among other issues.

Kawhi Leonard is set to return to Toronto for the upcoming season. (Getty Images: Patrick McDermott)

Leonard's trade to the Toronto Raptors has been on hold pending the outcome of the investigation. The Raptors had said they still want Leonard, and he apparently is just as eager to return to the team where he won an NBA title and was Finals MVP in 2019.

"As I return to Toronto, I am focused on what I can control, closing this chapter, and moving forward with a clean slate," Leonard said in his statement.

The Clippers and their personnel will be under a compliance and monitoring program by the league for five years and Robertson was banned from doing business with NBA teams for five years.

The league penalised Frank for his involvement with the impermissible endorsement arrangements and for approving impermissible expenses incurred by Leonard and his family.

Zucker was banned for being primarily and directly culpable for the illegal endorsement arrangements and for lying to investigators. Both will lose their salaries during their bans.

It is not the first time the Clippers have run afoul of NBA rules under Ballmer, who bought the team for $2 billion in August 2014.

They were fined $250,000 a year later for violating rules against offering unauthorised business or investment opportunities to players during their courting of free agent DeAndre Jordan. A presentation to him improperly included a $200,000-per-year deal with luxury car maker Lexus.

Ballmer, 70, was CEO of Microsoft from 2000 to 2014.

AP

title: How senior public servant's pro-stadium opinion piece was pushed through
text:
Less than two months before a final vote in parliament on the Macquarie Point stadium, Tasmania's coordinator-general, John Perry, entered the public debate.

The senior state service employee's intervention came in the form of a 3,000-word opinion piece published in Tasmania's major daily newspaper, The Mercury.

Mr Perry attempted to quantify the broader economic activity that would potentially stem from the state's then-promised $875 million spend.

His predicted economic return was more than six times greater than the government's own estimate.

"Can we really afford for the State not to make that investment?" he wrote.

The Macquarie Point stadium passed Tasmania's upper house in December, two months after John Perry's opinion piece was published. (Supplied: Cox Architecture)

The main role of Mr Perry's office is to attract private investment into the state.

But his public commentary on the stadium, prior to a parliamentary vote, prompted questions about whether he adhered to principles in the State Service Act to be "apolitical" and "impartial".

What was not known at the time was the extent of the role other interested parties played in helping to shape and promote Mr Perry's work, well before it was publicly released.

Emails obtained by the ABC — provided by his overarching department nine months after they were requested under right to information laws — show that draft copies of the piece went through a range of hands, including one of the main stakeholders: the Tasmania Devils AFL football club.

Football club involved in state servant's 'awesome work'

The piece came out in October 2025, but two months earlier, the football club was already involved in Mr Perry's work, emails show.

He was carrying out his own economic analysis on the stadium, sending Tasmania Football Club's marketing manager, Kathryn McCann, a "draft iteration of the narrative".

John Perry: As you can see, the narrative still needs a lot of refinement, further tidying and tweaking. Kathryn McCann: It's looking very useful. Want to make a time in the next week or so to regroup on this (awesome) work?

A month later, Mr Perry presented his modelling and analysis to the football club's senior executives and chair.

Kathryn McCann praised John Perry's stadium work multiple times during its development. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The next day, he wrote to Premier Jeremy Rockliff suggesting he would seek approval to publish an opinion piece on his modelling, "as I expect is required as a public servant".

No formal approval could be found under right to information laws; neither the government nor the Office of the Coordinator-General responded to a question about what form the approval was given, and if advice was sought.

State servant wanted to 'counterbalance' public commentary

As the piece developed, Mr Perry described his intention in multiple emails as being "to counterbalance the 'we can't afford the stadium'" commentary.

He sent a draft to Ms McCann, and two drafts to Master Builders Tasmania chief executive officer Jenna Cairney, who is a former communications director for the premier and past Mercury editor.

John Perry: Very keen for your thoughts and suggestions. Jenna Cairney: This is looking really really great. I'll have another stab of it overnight to try to get that first section down to a reasonable size for a large talking point/oped in the newspapers.

Ms Cairney wrote that she had "whipped up" a media release "for a news lead", while Ms McCann suggested incorporating further information — the content of which was redacted — and offered to assist in distributing it to media outlets.

A media release was ultimately not included, but the ABC understands it was pitched to media outlets as being fully Mr Perry's own work.

Jenna Cairney (left) was asked to provide feedback on multiple drafts of John Perry's opinion piece. (ABC News)

The Department of Premier and Cabinet (DPAC) also had a request.

The government was due to release its formal response to a scathing Tasmanian Planning Commission report on the stadium.

DPAC wanted Mr Perry's piece to be released to coincide with this.

Suggestion to brief 'key' upper house members

Three days before it was released, Mr Perry sent a draft copy to DPAC and the premier's office.

It included mark-ups and Ms Cairney's "general approach for releasing" it to the media.

Jeremy Rockliff was questioned about the opinion piece in parliament last year, but did not say when approval was given to John Perry. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Mr Perry also mentioned to Mr Rockliff's chief of staff that he would offer to brief "key" upper house members on his economic analysis.

At the time, the stadium looked set to pass the lower house with Labor's support, but the government needed the vote of at least three additional upper house members.

Briefings by department staff relating to bills are typically extended to all upper house members, rather than selected members; the ABC asked what was meant by "key" members and if it was appropriate for a state servant to make this political suggestion.

Neither the government nor the Office of the Coordinator-General responded to this question.

The suggestion for Mr Perry to brief these members appears to have originated with the Tasmania Football Club, emails show.

A briefing was not offered, according to at least one of the upper house members whose vote was required by the government.

Government argues Perry acted 'independently'

Mr Perry was questioned in a parliamentary hearing after the piece was published on October 11, saying it had not been requested by the government.

He was asked about who reviewed the work and analysis.

"I had shared internally just before it was released and I provided it the day that it was provided to others," Mr Perry said.

He said he had "sought some input" from people outside of government, and had talked to the football club.

John Perry was questioned about his opinion piece in a public accounts committee in parliament. (ABC News)

Mr Perry provided a written response in which he said he provided the "final version" to "people who have regular contact with the media".

The extent of the involvement of the Tasmania Football Club and Master Builders Tasmania — and the sharing of a draft with the government — was not disclosed in parliament, nor in the piece itself.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Coordinator-General said it had publicly supported other proposals. It is unclear if any of these were publicly funded.

"The office has undertaken various levels of analysis for a number of major investment proposals over the years and, where appropriate, provides official support for a proposal on the record," they said.

"Working collaboratively with relevant stakeholders to ensure timely material that is both to the point and factually correct is vital."

A government spokesperson said the work was done independently and was "in accordance with his duties".

"Attracting investment is what Mr Perry is employed to do," they said.

"Mr Perry independently undertook this work to assess how the stadium might impact Tasmania's economy."

Economic analysis faced scrutiny

The content of the opinion piece was also heavily scrutinised at the time.

Mr Perry argued the stadium would generate "at least $220.9m per year in new economic activity" at a cost of $44.5 million to finance the debt, a benefit of $4.97 for every $1 spent.

He wrote that other public commentary on the stadium had "questionable inclusions and startling omissions", and his office told the ABC his piece aimed to "address misinformation".

While being based on different methodologies, it was a vastly different figure to the government's estimate of 69 cents of benefit for every $1, and economist Nicholas Gruen's estimate of 44 cents per $1.

Independent upper house member Ruth Forrest described it as "when economic spin masquerades as analysis".

Dean Winter questioned John Perry's opinion piece, including how he reached a much higher level of economic benefit than other analyses. (ABC News)

Labor's Dean Winter was also critical, despite the party being in support of the stadium.

He argued that Mr Perry had double-counted interstate visitor activity and new hotel economic activity, which Mr Perry rejected.

"[This is] a piece of work, an editorial by a senior public servant, that isn't peer-reviewed, is not a cost-benefit analysis, it has double-counted spending," Mr Winter told parliament.

The stadium passed the upper house in December after several remaining independents supported it.

Work to remove about 100,000 cubic metres of soil from the waterfront site started in July.

The government intends to have it completed by the end of 2030, meaning the Tasmania Devils will play at least the first three seasons at Bellerive Oval and York Park.

The overall cost estimate remains at $1.13 billion, but an update could be provided once the construction tender process concludes.

title: Insurance delays as Exmouth residents struggle with living conditions
text:
Darryl Byatt and his family have been living in a shed for the last five months after Cyclone Narelle significantly damaged their home in March.

The Exmouth resident said he was fortunate that before the cyclone hit the town, 1,250 kilometres north of Perth, he renovated the shed so it was liveable for the short term.

Extensive damage made Darryl Byatt's house unliveable. (Supplied)

"The house was unliveable, the roof came off, the verandah came off and there was extensive damages to plasterboards and flooring," Mr Byatt said.

"We had concerns the insurance might take a little bit of time to process, we just did not expect five months," he said.

Not a unique situation

Cyclone Narelle was a category four system when it passed the coast of Exmouth, damaging homes, business, roads and the airport.

Mr Byatt said an assessment was done of his property by builders sent by his insurance company.

Darryl Byatt's property is still unsafe to live in five months after the damage. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

However, when Mr Byatt received the settlement quote he found a lot of the damage was missing from the report.

He said he questioned the insurer about why items were left out but could not get a definitive response.

"We declined to sign that thinking maybe we can get somewhere quickly and it's now been referred to Australian Financial Complaints Authority," he said.

" It just seems to be an extreme lack of follow-up and communication. "

Mr Byatt said his experience was not unique.

"I have spoken to a few people, there is different people with different insurance companies experiencing the same frustration," he said.

Some of the offered settlements seemed much below the actual repair costs while some cases failed to receive much response.

Several other property owners who had damage during the cyclone are experiencing similar issues. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

Challenging system

Exmouth Shire president Matt Niikkula said anybody with an insurance policy should be looked after.

"The insurance claims are obviously very high in volume and the insurance companies have to step up to the plate," Cr Niikkula said.

"Our expectation is they will look after each and every claim and make sure our community is not left in the dark."

Matt Niikkula says residents with policies deserved to be paid what they were entitled to in a timely manner. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

In the aftermath of the cyclone, the shire helped organise a team of legal aid lawyers to town to offer services not easily accessible in the remote location.

Regional Alliance West lawyer Dempsey Morgan visited Exmouth and said they wanted to ensure locals were aware of the obligations of insurance companies.

"We want to arm them with the knowledge so they know where to go from here," he said.

Mr Morgan said some insurance companies had hired builders from outside the town to conduct assessments and provide quotes.

Dempsey Morgan travelled to Exmouth to offer advice to residents. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

"Those quotes have come back higher than what the properties were insured for and that is leading to cash settlements," he said.

"Once people are accepting the cash settlement, there is a limited amount of funding available for alternative accommodation while works are completed."

A report released from the corporate watchdog, Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), earlier this week found at least 63 per cent of final home insurance claims included a cash settlement.

High volume of claims

Australian Insurance Council's director of Extreme Weather Response Liam Walter said more than 1,100 claims were reported from Exmouth following the cyclone, with more than 600 of them being household claims.

Houses in Exmouth suffered massive damages after Cyclone Narelle. (ABC News)

"I'd like to acknowledge the severity of the incident and the disruption it's caused and that we certainly understand what people are going through," Mr Walter said.

"Certainly the process can take some time and is really dependant on the damage."

He said while the properties with minor damages might have their claim settled, they expected five months waiting period for those with extensive damages.

"In some cases, it could be up to a year before their property is completely repaired," Mr Walter said.

He urged Exmouth locals to submit complaints to attract more attention to their case if they felt the insurers were not communicating appropriately.

"If things are not making sense or if requests are not being heard, then that complaints process is a really critical lever that customers have to kick their claim into a different path of review to try and get those issues resolved," Mr Walter said.

Following Mr Byatt's rejection of the quote, the insurance company has reached back out to him suggesting a re-assessment of his property.
