Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But increases in spending can also mean demand for goods outpaces supply, leading to price increases and contributing to inflation.

The hot GDP result could therefore add more pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to raise interest rates again as it struggles to close the gap between supply and demand.

Australia's cash rate target is currently 4.35 per cent following three rate hikes this year.

What does the data show?

Despite the impact of higher interest rates and the United States-Iran war, GDP growth accelerated on a quarterly basis from 0.3 per cent in March.

While the 2.1 per cent annual growth rate is faster than the RBA's assumed speed limit of 2 per cent, it was a subdued result by historical standards, as households continued to behave cautiously, ABS head of national accounts Grace Kim said.

"While increased spending and business investment occurred in pockets of the economy, imports supported much of the growth, moderating its contribution to overall GDP growth," she said.

Imports of goods rose 2.4 per cent, driven by increased purchases of cars and planes.

READ MORE November 'circled' as pivotal month for Aussie household budgets

Meanwhile, services imports fell 4.9 per cent as Australians' travel plans were disrupted by war in the Middle East.

"The number of Australians travelling overseas for the northern hemisphere summer fell for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, significantly reducing international travel expenditure," Kim said.

Household consumption rose 0.4 per cent, with falls in fuel consumption and travel due to higher fuel prices.

But the oil crisis also supported growth as consumers flocked to electric vehicles. EV purchases rose 10.3 per cent.

"The rise in electric vehicle purchases may have reflected households taking a longer-term approach to cost-of-living pressures, with some choosing EVs to help reduce ongoing expenses," Kim said.

Meanwhile, private business investment declined 0.5 per cent, due to a pullback in data centre investment.

GDP per capita was flat over the quarter, growing by 0.7 per cent over the 12 months to June.

Productivity was likewise flat but fell 0.2 per cent over the year.

Real unit labour costs — a measure closely watched by the Reserve Bank for signs of cost pressures on businesses — rose 0.9 per cent.

Impact on RBA

David Bassanese, chief economist at financial firm Betashares, said the "jury remains out on a September rate decision".

He described Wednesday's figures as slightly better than market expectations but still leaving Australia's economy "in a rut".

"The saving grace from the economic rut revealed by these numbers is they do not compel the RBA to raise rates, but they also do not rule out a hike in the future," he said in a statement.

"My base case is that September will not bring a rate increase, as the RBA will want to see more evidence on inflation and the moderation in house prices."

The RBA will next meet to discuss any changes to the cash rate target on 29 September.

title: Revealed: The failures behind Telstra's major network outage
text:
In brief An independent investigation has found Telstra failed to prioritise systems that led to a major outage.

A separate ACMA investigation, that could result in fines of up to $30 million, is ongoing.

Telstra did not prioritise systems that caused a major nationwide network failure and lacked the technical expertise to properly maintain them, an independent investigation has found.

The results of the review into the telco's 8 July network failure, which left thousands of Australians unable to make calls or access data, were released on Tuesday.

The outage sparked chaos with Triple Zero calls and businesses affected, along with failures across train networks and electronic payment services.

A lack of ownership and oversight of the functions that led to the outage were identified as key contributing factors by Technology Audit Partners in the report.

The outage began at 2.50am, nearly an hour earlier than identified by Telstra at the time.

Following the outage, Telstra confirmed it had conducted welfare checks on those who tried to place more than 600 unsuccessful emergency calls.

The investigation also found a further eight Triple Zero calls did not go through to emergency services during the outage. Welfare checks were conducted in relation to those unsuccessful calls, with no adverse outcomes identified, according to the company.

The outage was triggered by a software update not being done on a GPS card, which resulted in incorrect date information.

It was primarily a result of Telstra not treating network timing as a critical capability, the report found.

On the night of the outage, the two primary engineers involved in the botched upgrade were on mandatory stand-down, the report found.

"The overarching finding is we did not prioritise our timing system inside our networks at the highest level as a critical capability, which is exactly what it should have been," chief executive Vicki Brady told media on Wednesday.

"That is a miss on our side."

Brady said additional resources and expertise had been allocated to the impacted area.

Since the outage, just over 30,000 customers have contacted the telco, which has processed credits of just under $1 million for those customers.

Any customers who felt they were impacted and had not been in contact were encouraged to reach out to the company.

Brady was among 10 senior executives whose bonus was cut as a result of the outage. Her total compensation was $6.8 million, 11 per cent more than the previous year.

"I fully accept the board's decision on that," Brady said.

title: I've worked with families of missing people for 25 years. Here's how uncertainty feels
text:
The surging death count from the devastating flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on 26 August has passed 1,000.

At least 42 Australians are among more than 4,000 people still “unaccounted for”. But this phrase "unaccounted" — frequently used in media reports — can split the problem too simply: people are either lost or yet to be found.

For many families waiting for news, this gap between uncertainty and despair is ambiguous — and it’s agonising. There is no guarantee news will ever come.

So, how can people missing loved ones make sense of this traumatic experience while the search continues? And what kind of support will they need?

I have been working with families of missing people for more than 25 years. Here’s what I’ve learnt about their experiences of ambiguous loss.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What is ambiguous loss?

Ambiguous loss describes an ongoing loss without a resolution or closure. It can affect how people feel and behave, and the kind of support they will need.

While waiting for news of their loved ones in Nepal and Tibet, people will be grappling with the shock and trauma of how the disappearance unfolded, and the scale of the disaster. They will also be facing uncertainty and fear about how long they will be on this path.

When living with an ambiguous loss, it is common to oscillate between hopeful thinking and moments of hopelessness.

People may feel frozen to the time they learned the news, replay their last conversations with that person, or repetitively think up new ways to search and find them.

Families in Australia may also feel helpless being so far away, especially as the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has asked people to reconsider travelling to the affected areas to look for people who are out of contact. They may feel excluded from searching because they can’t travel to the region.

They may also experience physical and emotional agitation, feel sick in the stomach, or be restless from the need to constantly be on alert for information updates.

Validate both hope and hopelessness

When observing how people respond to a missing loved one, it can seem to others that families aren't embracing reality. This might look like clinging to ideas that someone is alive, against the odds, or hoping for a miracle in unlikely circumstances.

This isn’t a family’s decision to not confront the reality, but a normal response to incomprehensible and traumatic situations.

Social workers who work in the field of missing persons learn to encourage families to respond however they need— even if that changes minute by minute.

For many people, surges of hope sustain us in times of crisis and can be a strategy to survive uncertainty. Families not wanting to discuss the potential for a devastating outcome should not be framed as harboring "false hope", but as implementing a boundary that needs to be respected.

For others, there will be comfort in naming fears and imagining the worst. This allows them to voice the private stories that may be echoing in their minds, as they wait for news. While having someone missing is not a dress rehearsal for the grief that may be ahead, speaking the truth about the potential outcomes of a search, can make people feel less alone.

It’s important for people waiting for news to have safe spaces to discuss what they’re feeling and fearing, without judgement.

These private conversations might differ from public narratives (in the media or amid search efforts) which may focus on staying positive and be strength-based.

How to support families of missing people

Don’t speculate.

As a friend or supporter, it's not your job to tell people how to survive this moment. And speculating about possible outcomes can be cruel and unhelpful. Offering compassion and allowing yourself to be guided by what they say and want to talk about is key.

Don’t tell them to 'switch off'.

It may feel tempting to suggest friends or families turn away from traumatic news coverage. But this idea can feel impossible for those affected.

Instead, you could offer to consume news on their behalf, or take responsibility for answering phones or responding to messages. This may give them a small moment of respite.

READ MORE How Australians can help those impacted by devastating Nepal floods

Encourage them to channel their physical reactions to uncertainty.

People waiting for news, far away from the disaster, may be feeling agitated and constantly on alert. Even a short walk around the block or a few minutes of stretching can help manage the constant rush of adrenaline.

Sensory activities that ground you — such as naming something you can hear, see and feel — can also provide simple moments of certainty.

It’s OK to suggest self-care, but it’s best to do it gently and take their lead on what they might need. Attending to all of those activities that simply keep people functioning daily — sleeping, eating, showering — can also be important reminders.

The bottom line

When people are experiencing ambiguous loss, they need people around them to show compassion and be flexible, as they survive this moment. They may need to focus on just getting through the night, the hour, or even the next five minutes.

If you’re supporting someone waiting for news, take care of yourself too. For support options reach out to the National Missing Persons Coordination Centre, which is part of the Australian Federal Police.

Sarah Wayland is a professor of social work at CQUniversity Australia.

She has received funding from UNE to undertake research exploring media exposure for families of missing people. She is an interagency member of the Families and Friends of Missing Persons Unit and a non-executive board member for Missed Foundation.

title: The COVID trend Australia wasn't expecting this winter
text:
IN BRIEF COVID-19 cases are down 56 per cent on last year, despite infections beginning to rise again over the past fortnight.

Experts are pointing to population immunity and a more stable virus.

Australia appears to have avoided the winter surge in COVID-19 cases seen in previous years, according to a recent report.

Federal surveillance data shows 64,357 COVID-19 cases have been reported so far this year, 56 per cent fewer than the 146,232 cases recorded over the same period in 2025.

The latest figures paint an unusual picture of Australia's COVID-19 landscape, with infections remaining well below last year's levels even as cases begin to tick upwards across the community.

"In contrast to previous years, national data in 2026 to date do not yet show a clear winter peak," the Australian Centre for Disease Control said in its latest respiratory surveillance report.

Experts says changing virus behaviour and population immunity are possible explanations.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Where has the winter wave gone?

Professor Catherine Bennett, chair of epidemiology at Deakin University, said the absence of a clear winter peak was significant.

She said Australia's experience reflected a population that had gradually developed greater immunity to the virus through previous infections and vaccination.

"When you have variants that stay in circulation for a longer period of time, more people have had their immunity naturally boosted against that variant, and that then keeps infection rates down," she said.

Bennett said having fewer major changes in the variants circulating than earlier in the pandemic may be helping people's existing immunity provide greater protection against severe infection.

Rather than a substantially different variant emerging every few months in Australia, the same dominant variant was continuing to circulate, allowing immunity in the population to remain "primed".

Have COVID-19 patterns changed?

Epidemiologist professor Adrian Esterman told SBS News that the pattern of COVID-19 outbreaks had changed significantly over the past few years.

"We aren't actually seeing waves anymore, or if we do have waves they're very small ones," he said.

Esterman said smaller increases in cases now tended to coincide with the emergence of a variant that was better able to transmit or evade existing immunity.

The experts said that a major change to the virus' genetics could still trigger a larger wave, but said there was currently little evidence of one developing.

"Unless there's a huge genetic shift in the virus ... that's the only thing that could disrupt things and cause another wave," Esterman said.

Fewer cases detected

The sharp fall in reported cases raises the question of whether fewer Australians are getting COVID-19, or if fewer infections are being detected.

Reported COVID-19 cases are only a proportion of all infections, meaning surveillance data cannot capture every person who contracts the virus.

But Bennett said she believed the lack of a winter peak was broadly consistent with what was being seen in other measures of COVID-19 severity.

She pointed to hospitalisation data showing COVID-19 was now causing less severe disease among younger and healthier adults than earlier in the pandemic.

At the same time, she warned that there were still important gaps in Australia's understanding of the virus, particularly in relation to the longer-term consequences of infection.

Why immunity could be making a difference

Bennett said repeated exposure to COVID-19 may now be giving many people protection against severe illness without necessarily preventing them from becoming infected.

People may therefore experience very mild infections that are never detected, or fight off infections without becoming noticeably sick.

Bennett and Esterman told SBS News that if the same variants continue circulating, people who have previously encountered them may have enough immunity to prevent infections from producing the large rise in cases Australia has seen in previous winters.

"It's sort of keeping our immunity levels primed up naturally," Bennet said.

But she said that protection is not evenly distributed.

Bennett said older people and those who are immunocompromised may not develop the same strength of immune response from previous exposure, which is why vaccination remains important for those groups.

What happens as we head into spring?

According to the latest federal surveillance report, COVID-19 cases have started increasing again over the past fortnight.

But neither expert believes the rise signals the start of another major wave.

Bennett said the increase needed to be watched, particularly for evidence of a new variant gaining a foothold.

She said a new variant could potentially produce a summer surge, but there was currently no strong trend suggesting that was happening.

Esterman similarly expects the virus to continue producing relatively small increases in cases rather than the large, distinct waves seen earlier in the pandemic.

Could this become the new normal?

The absence of a winter peak does not mean COVID-19 has disappeared, or that future winters will necessarily look the same.

Both experts said that while Australia's 2026 experience could represent an important shift in the way COVID-19 behaves as an endemic respiratory virus, a significant change in the virus could alter the current pattern.

Bennett said the combination of declining transmission, population immunity and a more stable virus had put Australia in a much stronger position than it was in the early years of the pandemic.

"It's very unusual but an important sign that our population-level immunity is still evolving and maturing and putting us in a much better position to cope with an endemic disease like COVID-19."

And if the current trend continues through the warmer months, she said Australia could be entering its quietest 12-month period of COVID-19 transmission in years.

"If we can get through summer without another wave, then that will be the best 12 months we've had for a long time with COVID-19."

title: What's behind the 'biggest oil deal in world history' Trump is touting with Venezuela?
text:
In Brief Donald Trump says the US has signed an agreement that gives the US a stake in Venezuelan oil reserves.

The deal has been thrown into question by experts who question its legal and economic validity.

Details are emerging about what United States President Donald Trump is calling "the biggest oil deal in world history" with Venezuela.

Trump said the agreement announced on Saturday would give the US a stake in Venezuela's vast oil reserves, a step toward his goal of extracting energy from the country after US forces captured then-president Nicolás Maduro in a middle-of-the-night raid in January and brought him to New York to face federal drug trafficking charges.

Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, described the deal as a step toward economic recovery that will modernise the country’s oil industry.

In a televised address to the nation on Sunday, Rodríguez insisted Venezuela's sovereignty is secure and said she wants the country to become a global energy powerhouse.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

On Tuesday, the White House released a fact sheet about the arrangement.

Here's a look at what's known about the deal — and what remains unclear.

What are the terms?

The US government and a private operator in Venezuela have formed a new company that has been granted rights to access untapped oil fields for 100 years.

A statement from Rodríguez said the deal involves the development of 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels.

It said the agreement could draw US$100 billion ($139 billion) in investment into Venezuela's oil industry and yield over US$209 billion ($291 billion) in taxes for the country.

The private operator is North America Blue Energy Partners, owned by Alejandro Betancourt, the White House confirmed on Tuesday.

The company currently produces about 200,000 barrels a day, which makes it the second-largest private operator in Venezuela behind Chevron, according to a source who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to release the information.

Trump said the agreement was negotiated by US secretary of state Marco Rubio, defence secretary Pete Hegseth and Rodríguez.

The deal will give the US a 35 per cent ownership stake in the company, and the US state department will get a guarantee to buy 20 per cent of the output at cost. US purchases of oil will go towards US strategic oil reserves along with the military, according to a US official who was not authorised to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The company would be the second largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, according to the US official.

Bob McNally, who was an energy adviser in former US president George W Bush's administration, said the current administration appears to be seeking ways to make it easier for the private sector to invest in Venezuela's industry through the deal.

"However, investors will remain cautious even if the terms of the deal, once released, pass legal muster. A future president could withdraw, and Caracas has twice thrown foreign investors out," McNally said.

Amos Hochstein, who was a senior energy adviser to former US president Joe Biden, said the deal is uncharted territory from a legal and diplomatic perspective.

It carries tremendous risk for companies thinking about doing business under the new arrangement, he said. Democrats could challenge the deal if they regain power in the US, as could future administrations in Venezuela.

"There will be a lot of challenges to what was just announced," Hochstein said. "I can only say, if it were me, I'd be nervous. And if I'm back in my old job in the next administration, then they should be nervous."

How have Venezuelans reacted?

Some in Venezuela have considered the deal a betrayal of what their government has stated repeatedly for decades: Venezuelan resources are for Venezuela, and leaders would not allow the US government access to those resources.

Harvard University professor Ricardo Hausmann, a former Venezuelan planning minister, called it a "shameful deal".

"Venezuelans will not respect this illegitimate deal and no major US oil company will take it seriously because they know it will not last,” Hausmann said on social media, adding that Rodríguez "has no legitimacy or constitutional power to commit Venezuela to any such deal".

In her national address, Rodríguez pushed back on some early criticism.

"One thing must be absolutely clear: Venezuela retains ownership and sovereignty over its resources," Rodríguez said.

She said the goal is to reach other agreements with transnational private companies such as Chevron, Repsol and Shell.

What's the reaction in the US?

It is unclear whether US congress will play a role in the arrangement, but politicians from both parties were quick to weigh in. Trump allies called it a win.

Republican senator Bernie Moreno said it was a historic deal that would help both countries.

"If it were up to DC Democrats, Maduro would still be in power, Venezuelan oil would be going to China at half price, and the people of Venezuela would be getting robbed by a corrupt regime," Moreno said in a post on social media.

It was widely condemned by Democrats who said Maduro's capture was a means to this end.

What questions remain?

Many important details remain unclear, including who will cover necessary investments and how America's stake in the company breaks down.

The US will get 55 per cent of the company's effective output, but it was not clear what portion of that comes from an ownership stake and how much comes from the right to buy oil at cost.

It is also unclear how the industry will react. Persuading big US oil companies to return to the region could prove challenging given the political uncertainty and damaged infrastructure.

READ MORE Why Australia ships out its wealth — and buys it back as finished goods

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said that on its face, the deal could double US oil reserves and reduce dependence on crude oil from Canada and Mexico.

But Oxley, writing in a commentary, cautioned that there are logistical hurdles and said the value of Venezuela's reserves may have been exaggerated under former Venezuelan president Hugo Chávez.

Even with legal and security guarantees, it is not clear that US oil companies "would be eager to invest", he wrote, noting that "there simply might be more enticing commercial opportunities on offer elsewhere".

title: SBS confirmed as Australia's home of the 2030 FIFA World Cup
text:
IN BRIEF: SBS has secured exclusive rights to broadcast the 2030 World Cup live and free to all Australians.

The agreement strengthens a 40-year relationship between SBS and FIFA.

SBS has cemented its place as Australia’s spiritual home of football, securing exclusive national rights to the FIFA World Cup 2030.

Football-loving Australians will have access to all 104 matches of the 2030 tournament via SBS television, video and radio programming.

SBS managing director Jane Palfreyman said the broadcaster is "without question" Australia’s home of the World Cup.

"The FIFA World Cup is one of the few sporting events that truly brings Australians together across all cultures, languages and communities," she said.

"In 2030 audiences will once again be able to experience every match live and free on SBS."

The bacteria is spread through contact with the waste of infected animals and can cause bloody diarrhoea and lead to kidney failure. The parents said their daughter had also tested positive for RSV and parainfluenza in the days after being admitted to hospital. The Age has chosen not to name the farm, as health experts have said the bacteria is present in most farms and there is no evidence this one has acted inappropriately. It’s understood that an investigation by local health authorities has cleared the farm of any wrongdoing. Local health authorities advised the farm to increase handwashing stations and to display a sign at its entrance warning of the risk of infection and the importance of handwashing.

Advertisement

More than 160 cases of Shiga toxin-producing E.coli or STEC (the bacteria that causes the rare condition) have been recorded across the state this year, compared with 156 cases for all of 2023. If this trend continues, Victoria’s latest figures will eclipse the 235 cases recorded last year. Deputy Chief Health Officer Dr Clare Looker previously told this masthead that the department had not yet identified a common source for the reported HUS cases. “The Department of Health investigates all reported cases of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) to identify potential sources of infection and prevent further cases,” she said.

Advertisement

Looker said the increase in recorded STEC cases was linked to improved testing and reporting practices. HUS is often triggered by the Shiga toxin entering a person’s blood and creating small blood clots that block the kidneys, causing them to “shut off”. Parents should seek medical attention if their children have pus or blood in their stools, reduced urine output, lethargy, pale lips or small dots on their skin. Children under the age of five, as well as those with suppressed immune system, are particularly susceptible.

Advertisement

Transmission occurs through exposure to animals, particularly cattle, and by eating undercooked meat and drinking unpasteurised milk. To prevent infection, children’s hands should be washed after any contact with animals, ideally with soap and water. Meat should be thoroughly cooked, and fruit and vegetables should be washed before consumption. In 2014, a three-year-old Victorian boy died from organ failure after consuming raw, unpasteurised milk that contained STEC. Be the first to know when major news happens. Every restaurant featured in The Age Good Food Guide 2026 in Melbourne’s Northern Suburbs. See all stories .

Roll up your sleeves: things are about to get saucy. Almost everything at this colourful eatery – a Mexico City native’s taste of home – is made to be held. The torta, Mexico’s national sandwich, is among our city’s finest: crusty bolillo rolls are ugly-delicious with hunks of aromatic, fall-apart beef brisket plus melted Oaxaca cheese coating the outside.

Guajillo chilli-marinated pork tacos are so stacked and sauced they’ll spatter your pastel-hued plate, while the lamb barbacoa tacos are a Friday-to-Sunday specialty served with consomme. A metres-high sign on the frontage spruiks the signature dish: pozole, a deeply nourishing soup seldom seen in Melbourne, fragrant with oregano and bobbing with chewy hominy (maize kernels).

What El Columpio lacks in frills, it makes up for in high-calibre Mexican thrills, offering freewheeling good times with mezcal-spiked cocktails – and the occasional mariachi band.

SportRacingHorse racing They’re racing at Randwick on Saturday. These are the horses that will win Ray Hickson September 3, 2026 — 1:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Race 1: MIDWAY HANDICAP (1400M) 1. Felix Majestic has run himself back into form in stronger races and is in a Midway where there doesn’t appear to be a lot of competition for the front. Don’t mind him drawn out a bit as he’s taken 100m or so to wind up out of the gates, if that early part works out for him he’s a big chance to break through. 16. Vexxy is eligible for much easier races but she showed she’s up to this grade already with a slashing fifth in the 1200m Midway a couple of weeks ago. Interesting to see if she can back it up from a much better gate. 3. Dusty Bay reacted really well to being ridden off the speed when scoring at Warwick Farm three runs back. Just fair at Rosehill last time out when he hit the front early in the straight and boxed on well for third. Every chance with the smother draw. 4. Long Legs was expected to fare better when resuming two weeks ago, she may have had some excuses, but a couple got past her late. Better off at this trip, blinkers on, so she could be an improver.

How to play it: Felix Majestic to win. Race 2: BUY YOUR KOSCIUSZKO TICKETS AT TAB HIGHWAY HANDICAP (1200M) 4. Mrs Goldberg was nothing short of dominant in scoring first-up in the Highway two weeks ago. She did have a nice run just ahead of the midfield but you couldn’t be anything but impressed with how she put them away. Similarly drawn and 1200m holds no fears. Hard to beat. 11. Lord Remlap is a promising type unbeaten in three starts including a Highway in April, where he almost threw it away. Barrier is a worry but he’s trialling well and with a bit of luck, he’s a threat. 20. Empress Tsarina stuck to her guns when chasing Mrs Goldberg in her best performance. Draws kindly and she’s an each-way chance. 2. Wayburn is another drawn a shade awkwardly, but he reacted well to being ridden off the pace when scoring at Rosehill five weeks ago. In the mix.

How to play it: Mrs Goldberg to win. Race 3: LAUREL OAK SUPPORTER OF NJT HANDICAP (1100M)

Advertisement

9. Scenic Point was heavily backed before being a late scratching at the barriers from a Warwick Farm engagement a few weeks ago. Back to the trials and looked pretty slick. She was a Listed winner last year for the previous stable and on what we’ve seen from her trials she can be a major player. 1. Kimberley Secrets continues to race well in this company. A game second at Rosehill last week when she tried hard to run down Oh Arthur and just failed. She’ll put herself there and give a good sight again. 3. Ernaux comes back 100m from her past few starts which have realised a win and two seconds. Racing well and drawn to get the last shot at them, which is very much her most effective style. 7. Island Dec is resuming from a two-month absence and she’s the type that could blouse them late, as she did at Canterbury two starts ago, with the right sort of run.

How to play it: Scenic Point to win. Race 4: DRINKWISE CUP (2400M) Thebudgiesmugla has an imposing record. Getty Images 1. Thebudgiesmugla brings an imposing 2400m record of five from five into this and that makes him tough to beat. Would love a bit more sting out of the ground for him, but he was more than acceptable fresh in the Premiers Cup at 2000m, has a positive racing style and he runs the trip. 2. So You Are has done battle with his now stablemate three times and has a 1-2 record with the Premiers Cup his first “victory” as he ran a handy second. Has that habit of finding one or two better but in a race of few chances on paper he will be right there. 3. Sam Hawkens faces something of a D-Day. He’s been disappointing since he arrived about a year ago and couldn’t keep up with the tempo on speed fresh a month ago. Much better suited at this trip and he’s entitled to show something. 5. Fernao is racing well in Brisbane of late with three seconds on end. Started $71 when he last raced Thebusdgiesmugla but back down in the weights he’s a chance.

How to play it: Thebudgiesmugla to win. Race 5: TAB HANDICAP (1200M)

Advertisement

3. Alabama State is due a change of luck after two good runs from a spell in similar races. Trapped wide second-up back in the field in a slowly run race and has kept coming to be beaten a length. Draws a little better this time, should be nice and fit. Does prefer a dry track. Good each-way prospect. 14. Off The Press ran a promising race when resuming at Rosehill with a close second and he has won three from four when second-up. Can see him getting a nice run and no surprise to see him in the finish. 20. Rose Aye was hard in the market when she resumed a month ago, she led and knocked up a bit late when running fifth behind Ernaux. She’ll be fitter for it, won’t have to work as hard from the draw and is worth considering. 2. Bartolf wasn’t disgraced despite never being a winning chance first-up two weeks ago. Can improve quickly.

How To Play It: Alabama State each-way. Race 6: KIA ORA STUD FURIOUS STAKES (1200M) Pembrey cruises to victory in the Silver Shadow Stakes. Getty Images 2. Pembrey was impressive winning the Silver Shadow first-up against several of her rivals in this. She ran fast and didn’t look like stopping. It’s quite a benchmark to set for returning to the same track and distance. If she has improvement in her then she’ll probably be too slick again. 3. Chilly Girl is new opposition for Pembrey and she was very good in her own right winning the Rosebud, running down Blue Door. Drawn to stalk and is the logical danger. Can’t wait to see 6. Bangkok Hottie at 1400m and beyond. She was excellent running on from the back in the Silver Shadow into second and we can expect something similar. 1. Chayan started favourite in the Golden Slipper after she won the Reisling Stakes in a canter. She’s since been sold for $5.6 million. Not sure where she finds herself from the outside but she’s looking in good order and will improve.

How To Play It: Pembrey to win. Race 7: MYPLATES TRAMWAY STAKES (1400M)

Advertisement

7. Idle Flyer is not a noted first-up performer so her effort in the Winx Stakes is more than a pass mark in the context of this race. She’s won four from four second-up and while she stays at 1400m you’d argue this is a step back in grade, despite some quality opposition, and if she’s within a couple coming up the rise will be tough to hold out. 5. Private Eye is a marvel. Tried hard when runner-up to Cosmic Crusader in the PB Lawrence at Caulfield and while drawn the outside here he might just get a favour or two up front. A top four finish sees him pass $13m in prizemoney and you’d imagine he’ll achieve that at least. 3. Attica was more than acceptable first-up behind the in-form Althoff. He was a solid favourite there and while he couldn’t match the winner’s dash with 7kg less it was a good starting point. Fitter and he can be dangerous. 1. Headley Grange can’t be discounted, he was excellent without winning against the A grade in the Sydney autumn before his Group 1 win in Brisbane. Definite chance.

How To Play It: Idle Flyer to win. Race 8: CATANACH’S JEWELLERS CONCORDE STAKES (1000M) Napoleonic running second to Tempted in the Eskimo Prince Stakes in February. Getty Images 4. Tempted on top and while she might be a little vulnerable with 58kg at the short trip fresh we know she’s a high-class mare. Only defeat in six starts at Randwick was at the hands of Ka Ying Rising in the TAB Everest last year, not a bad recommendation. She’s trialling well, unbeaten first-up and drawn perfectly. 1. Headwall won this race last year and hasn’t raced since. He’s had a solid grounding with four trials since June and should have reasonable fitness levels. Six of his seven wins are at 1000m so he’s in his zone. 2. Marhoona won the Galaxy in the autumn and she’s also resuming since the Arrowfield where she ran fourth behind Tempted. She was narrowly beaten in the Challenge over this course in March. Sure to be competitive as always. 5. Roselyn’s Star has a bit of race fitness from an impressive win in the July Sprint six weeks ago. Trialled sharply and while this is the toughest race he’s contested, he has a great record.

How To Play It: Tempted to win. Race 9: ASAHI SUPER DRY CHELMSFORD STAKES (1600M)

Advertisement

Nash Rawiller riding Lindermann to win the Chelmsford Stakes at Randwick in September 2025. Getty Images 2. Lindermann has a lovely set up to bounce back to form after a below par run in the Winx Stakes first-up. He did something similar a year ago before beating Sir Delius in this race. Hard to knock his autumn form despite not winning, placings to Autumn Glow and Aeliana before being runner-up in the Queen Elizabeth ahead of Autumn Glow. Had a brilliant spring last year, he’s a dry tracker and will take running down. 1. Ceolwulf tends to keep improving through his preparation but he started his spring with an excellent fifth in the Winx, attacking the line nicely. Doesn’t look a fast race on paper which might be against him but he is entitled to be breathing down their necks. 7. Green Spaces will excel at 2000m and above, but he too was excellent in the Winx picking up some late ground at the end of the 1400m. No shock if he’s in the first four home. 9. Fangirl was disappointing in the Winx. She’s been a wonderful mare over many seasons, she’ll need to lift on that last run but you’ve got to have concerns. Anywhere near her best and she goes close.

How To Play It: Lindermann to win. Race 10: THE AGENCY REAL ESTATE HANDICAP (1600M) 9. The Mona Lisa has been a revelation in the past couple of months and while she’s up in class she has found another winnable race over the Randwick mile. She had to do a lot of chasing behind a tearaway leader when we last saw her a month ago and she picked him up and was still strong to the line. Gets some weight relief and has the tactical ability to offset the gate. Can’t see her doing anything else but running well. 8. Starzintheireyes might turn out to be the best horse here over a bit more ground but 1600m gives him a big chance to post his first local win. He couldn’t be trialling better leading into this and any support would be a significant pointer. 13. Watson has gate one which might help him after working a bit in the Goulburn Cup early from a wider gate. He didn’t dash when he hit the front and that’s a little concern but entitled to another chance. 10. Starphistocated comes through the same race and she drew the outside there and was never in the hunt. Runner-up at Group 3 mares level over the Randwick mile in March.

How To Play It: The Mona Lisa each-way. Supplied by Racing NSW

title: ‘Name of the game’: De Minaur adapts to New York deluge with fast win
text:

Updated SportTennisUS Open ‘Name of the game’: De Minaur adapts to New York deluge with fast win Marc McGowan Updated September 3, 2026 — 12:57pm ,first published September 3, 2026 — 5:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur had to wait until the fourth day of the US Open to play his first match. Fifty minutes later, he was off court again. New York’s wet weather continues to wreak havoc with the tournament’s first week as Australia’s world No.7, who was supposed to start his campaign on Wednesday (AEST), endured another rain delay before returning to blitz Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri 6-2, 6-2, 6-4. Alex de Minaur finally progressed to the second round after days of rain delays at the US Open. AP De Minaur broke Guerrieri – playing his first grand slam main draw match at age 27 – in the first game of each of the first two sets and appeared poised for a quick passage to the second round until weather intervened. He led 6-2, 4-2 when the chair umpire suspended play, with the delay lasting about two hours before he joined fellow Australians Dane Sweeny, Tristan Schoolkate, Taylah Preston, Kim Birrell, Maya Joint, Alexei Popyrin and James Duckworth as a first-round winner.

Advertisement

De Minaur needed only 99 minutes either side of the latest rain disruption to demolish his left-handed rival, looking sharp with his ball-striking and movement from the outset, albeit with a slight detour in the third set. With the finish line in sight, the three-time US Open quarter-finalist threw in a sloppy service game that he lost to love when trying to push 4-2 ahead. He also slipped 0-30 behind his next time with the Wilson balls before getting back on track to complete his victory. Loading “These tournaments, it’s all about adapting – and that’s the name of the game,” de Minaur said. “There’s too much to play for to let something like this affect you, so I’m glad [about how] I handled it. I’m glad I got in and out, played a relatively clean match, and now I can focus on the next one.

Advertisement

“Because of the rain, there’s nothing you can do about it. You’ve just got to get out there, play your tennis match and, ultimately, if you win enough matches, you’re going to get out on the stadium court. So that’s the mindset.” But it was a tough day for de Minaur’s fellow Australians despite gallant performances from Joint and Birrell against seeded opponents. It has been a wet and wild week for tennis fans in New York. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth Joint, who spoiled Serena Williams’ much-anticipated singles comeback at Wimbledon, took a set off a top-10 foe for the first time, but could not sustain her hard-hitting onslaught as she fell 6-2, 7-6 (8-6), 6-4 to four-time major semi-finalist Elina Svitolina. The 20-year-old had an extended form slump this year, but produced spectacular tennis at times against the No.9 seed, particularly in the second set – which she twice led by a break – and still looks the country’s best prospect.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

US Open From GoFundMe to making big bank: Australian’s US Open breakthrough Joint was ranked inside the top 30 in February before losing 13 of 14 matches, including 10 in a row, but has righted the ship. Birrell, 28, staged a mid-match fightback against No.18 seed Ekaterina Alexandrova to force a third set, but a double fault on the first point led to her immediately handing the initiative to her Russian rival before eventually going down 6-1, 2-6, 6-3. Three other compatriots were far less competitive. Twenty-year-old wildcard Preston was trounced 6-1, 6-1 in 48 minutes by American Taylor Townsend in her second-round match, hitting only two winners compared to 28 unforced errors, while veteran James Duckworth lost 7-5, 6-3, 6-1 to China’s Wu Yibing.

Advertisement

Daria Kasatkina is also out, losing her rain-interrupted first-round clash with Spain’s former world No.2 Paula Badosa that was carried over from the previous day. Badosa was only two points from victory when the match was paused, and had to stave off two break-back points before clinching a 6-1, 5-4 win on her ninth match point to lock in a showdown with 2024 champion Coco Gauff. Australia’s Taylah Preston has been knocked out in the second round. Getty Images Pushed out to Flushing Meadows’ back blocks on court 11, after originally being scheduled on the bigger Grandstand stadium a day earlier, de Minaur did not have the fortune of playing on one of the event’s two courts with a retractable roof. The challenges for de Minaur rise steeply from here – beginning in the second round with dangerous Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp, who advanced in straight sets against Brit Jan Choinski.

Advertisement

Van de Zandschulp famously upset Carlos Alcaraz in the second round at the US Open two years ago. Related Video Video icon 0:50 Demon smashes through to second round De Minaur’s projected rivals beyond that are 31st seed Zizou Bergs (third round) and top seed Alexander Zverev (quarter-finals), who needed almost five hours to battle past Italy’s Lorenzo Sonego in the first round. However, his potential path was made somewhat easier when possible fourth-round opponent, in-form No.12 seed Rafael Jodar, suffered a shock 6-2, 6-1, 6-1 loss to lucky loser Bu Yunchaokete, who entered the draw when Australia’s Thanasi Kokkinakis withdrew with an ankle issue. After a brilliant start to the season, including a second straight Australian Open quarter-final and winning the Rotterdam title, de Minaur has relatively struggled, at least by his lofty standards.

Advertisement

He will hope to return to at least the last eight again in New York after losing in the third and fourth rounds at Roland-Garros and Wimbledon, respectively. World No.1 Aryna Sabalenka, 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev, Marta Kostyuk, Stefanos Tsitsipas and Americans Jessica Pegula, Ben Shelton, Frances Tiafoe and Iva Jovic were among the big names to make the round of 32. Carlos Alcaraz’s comeback is also gathering steam, ousting Portugal’s Jaime Faria 4-6, 6-0, 6-3, 6-2. With AAP News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. title: Lindian inks 20-year offtake deal for Kazakhstan rare earths product
text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Lindian inks 20-year offtake deal for Kazakhstan rare earths product Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd September 3, 2026 — 12:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Soon-to-be rare earths producer Lindian Resources has inked a binding strategic partnership with French rare earths specialist Carester, locking in an offtake agreement for up to 20 years and kicking off plans for a major downstream oxide separation facility in Kazakhstan. The deal provides a long-term home for Lindian’s heavy rare earths production and represents a major step in the company’s vertically integrated “mine-to-oxide” strategy. A concept design of Carester’s Caremag plant in France, where Lindian Resources will send its heavy rare earths product for refining. The offtake agreement has an initial 10-year term with options for two five-year extensions. Under the deal, Carester will purchase 70 per cent of the mixed heavy rare earth carbonate (MHREC) produced at Lindian’s SARECO processing facility in Kazakhstan. The heavy rare earths product will be supplied as feedstock to the Caremag refinery in Lacq, France – a joint venture development between Carester, the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security and Iwatani Corporation.

Advertisement

‘Carester brings both world-class separation expertise and a long-term route to market for our heavy rare earth production.’ Lindian Resources executive chairman Robert Martin The French facility has already secured substantial government funding from both France and Japan, effectively plugging Lindian into a well-funded, major Western-aligned critical minerals supply chain. The agreement with Carester also triggers the next phase of Lindian’s downstream ambitions. The two companies will now push forward with a definitive feasibility study (DFS) for a new 8000-tonne-per-annum solvent extraction and oxide separation facility at Stepnogorsk in Kazakhstan. The new plant will be designed to produce magnet-quality neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide at greater than 99.5 per cent purity, in addition to the heavy rare earths already destined for France. The study is slated to wrap up by year’s end. Lindian Resources executive chairman Robert Martin said: “Carester brings both world-class separation expertise and a long-term route to market for our heavy rare earth production. Its Caremag facility is backed by $350 million of French and Japanese funding and is targeting approximately 15 per cent of global dysprosium and terbium oxide production, demonstrating the strategic importance of the supply chain that we are building.”

Advertisement

The company’s downstream push is underpinned by Lindian’s cornerstone asset, the giant Kangankunde rare earths operation in Malawi. The project hosts a massive mineral resource of 261 million tonnes grading an impressive 2.19 per cent total rare earth oxides (TREO). Stage one construction at Kangankunde is already well advanced and, importantly, fully funded thanks to a recent $100 million institutional placement and supplementary local financing in Malawi. First production of premium monazite concentrate from the project is scheduled for later this year. The finished product will then be shipped to Lindian’s SARECO processing facility in Kazakhstan, where it will be processed ready for final separation at the proposed new oxide facility. The plan to build out the new separation plant has also received a significant vote of confidence from the Kazakhstan Government, with the Ministry of Industry and Construction recognising the project as strategically important to the nation’s downstream ambitions. Lindian says the new facility will need no outside funding, instead being organically funded from cash flows from its Kangankunde and SARECO operations.

Advertisement

The move into separated oxides should allow the company to capture significantly more value from its resource. The heavy rare earth elements dysprosium and terbium, which will be sold to Carester, command exceptionally high prices compared to concentrate products and are vital for high-performance permanent magnets used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. With its world-class Kangankunde project backed by a long-term offtake arrangement with Iluka Resources and now a pathway to high-value separated oxides secured through its partnership with Carester, Lindian is methodically assembling all the pieces of a significant rare earths production business. For a junior miner to be building a mine in Africa, a hydromet plant in Central Asia and now an oxide separation facility — all while fully funded for the first stage — is no small feat. The Carester deal appears to be the final piece of a complex puzzle that could see Lindian leap from aspiring developer to a meaningful force in the global rare earths supply chain. title: Critical data dive uncovers three NZ gold-antimony targets
text:
Advertisement

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Critical data dive uncovers three NZ gold-antimony targets Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 3, 2026 — 12:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Critical Resources has defined three new priority gold and antimony targets at its Silver Peaks project in New Zealand after a deep dive into historical exploration data. The review has zeroed in on the Lamb Hill-Three O’Clock, Stone Burn South and Northern Soil Anomaly targets, all lying within the company’s 497.69-square-kilometre prospecting permit in the prolific Otago region. Critical’s Silver Peaks project, which forms part of the company’s 1694-square-kilometre NZ footprint, sits immediately south of the Hyde-Macraes Shear Zone, a geological beast that hosts OceanaGold’s Macraes gold camp, New Zealand’s largest active gold operation with a resource of more than 10 million ounces. Critical Resources has defined three priority gold-antimony targets at its Silver Peaks project in New Zealand. The company’s review sifted through more than 1250 historical soil and stream-sediment records, identifying three distinct areas where historical mineral occurrences, anomalous geochemistry and favourable structures appear to coincide. Notably, the review found no evidence of any historical drilling at the three new target areas, leaving them untested by modern methods. The highest-priority target, Lamb Hill-Three O’Clock, combines a six-sample gold-arsenic stream anomaly with two historical antimony lode occurrences. Regional interpretation suggests these features sit within a broader northwest-trending structural corridor that could extend for up to 10km.

Advertisement

‘The historical review has resolved a large permit-scale dataset into three clear areas that can now be tested.’ Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither Historical stream sampling at the target returned up to 13 parts per billion (ppb) gold and 34 parts per million (ppm) arsenic, while the two historical antimony lodes were described as being about 1.5 metres thick. The combination of structure, stream geochemistry and known mineralisation makes it a potentially compelling walk-up target. The Stone Burn South target has been bolstered by two generations of historical geochemistry. Old BHP stream-sediment sampling from the late 1980’s returned solid results of 45.2 and 39.3ppb gold from separate catchments. More recent soil sampling then identified a supporting arsenic-antimony response, with results up to 68ppm arsenic and 17ppm antimony. The third target, the Northern Soil anomaly, is defined by a cluster of gold-arsenic soil results, including a composite sample grading 16ppb gold with 34ppm arsenic. A separate historical soil site in the same area also returned impressive results of 57.5 and 58.5ppb gold from coarse and fine fractions. Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither said: “The historical review has resolved a large permit-scale dataset into three clear areas that can now be tested efficiently in the field. At the Northern Soil Anomaly, gold and arsenic occur together across several composite samples, while Stone Burn South combines earlier gold-in-stream results with later arsenic and antimony pathfinder geochemistry. At Lamb Hill-Three O’Clock, the historical geochemistry and antimony occurrences lie within a broader northwest-trending structural setting that provides a clear focus for field mapping and systematic sampling.”

Advertisement

The new findings look well timed, with gold holding above A$6000 and antimony now firmly established as a strategic critical mineral, attracting significant geopolitical and market interest. New Zealand’s gold-antimony belt has also been enjoying something of a renaissance, drawing fresh attention from investors and developers. Further to the northwest, Critical is progressing a suite of gold projects. At its Cap Burn and Rock and Pillar projects, first-pass reverse circulation (RC) drilling has already confirmed structurally controlled gold mineralisation, with a follow-up drill program now in planning. Meanwhile, the company is conducting desktop reviews for drill targeting at its Tokomairiro gold project in the country’s south. Alongside sharpening its focus on gold and antimony in New Zealand, the company continues to advance its flagship Mavis Lake lithium project in Canada, which hosts a JORC-compliant resource of eight million tonnes (Mt) grading 1.07 per cent lithium oxide. Notably, the company has also defined a much bigger JORC-compliant exploration target at the project of between 18 and 29Mt at a grade of 0.8 to 1.2 per cent lithium oxide, pointing to significant growth potential across the company’s recently increased 400-square-kilometre landholding. Additionally, to help optimise and scale up its novel Dry Supersonic Deposition battery manufacturing technology, Critical has brought in the heavy hitters, launching a collaborative research project with Australia’s national science agency, the CSIRO, demonstrating a multi-pronged approach to the critical minerals space.

Advertisement

The company is now planning a more detailed field program at Silver Peaks to verify and rank the three targets. The work will involve geological mapping and modern surface geochemistry using a gold-antimony-arsenic-tungsten analytical suite. Any progression to geophysics or drilling would depend on the results and require a separate minerals exploration permit. title: ‘Sailor’s disease’ scurvy linked to young boy’s death
text:
Advertisement

NationalQueenslandHealth ‘Sailor’s disease’ scurvy linked to young boy’s death Robyn Wuth September 3, 2026 — 12:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A six-year-old Brisbane boy has died from scurvy, the so‑called “sailor’s disease” common in the convict era. Connor Dean died after a cardiac arrest under general anaesthetic at Queensland Children’s Hospital in 2024. The boy was admitted to Queensland Children’s Hospital in July, and died less than a month later. Brisbane Times Two years later, Deputy State Coroner Stephanie Gallagher has released her findings, ruling the child’s fatal brain damage was most likely triggered by vitamin C deficiency and scurvy. “Although the precise mechanism leading to the cardiac arrest could not be definitively determined, the treating clinicians and forensic pathologist considered vitamin C deficiency to be the most likely underlying factor,” she determined.

Advertisement

Issues with an unnamed multivitamin were also canvassed. Scurvy was once common among sailors and convicts who went without fresh fruit and vegetables on long sea voyages. However, it is now so rare in Australia that serious cases are almost always found and treated. Connor had Down syndrome, was born with a serious heart defect that was repaired in 2018, and had delayed development, speaking mostly in single words and walking with a wide gait. By July 2024, he had about three weeks of worsening leg pain.

Advertisement

He was admitted to hospital on July 18, with X‑rays and MRIs failing to show a clear cause. He then developed a bad cough and tested positive for parainfluenza as his oxygen levels and kidney function worsened. Scans of his skeleton later showed bone changes “in keeping with scurvy”. Blood tests revealed a vitamin C level of less than one micromole a litre, compared with a normal range of 20 to 120 micromoles a litre. He was also low in vitamins A and E, had borderline low vitamin D and blood‑clotting problems that suggested vitamin K deficiency.

Advertisement

Connor never recovered from the brain damage after the cardiac arrest and died on August 10. His paediatrician told the court he and dietitians had long‑standing concerns about the boy’s growth, with his height and weight well below the usual range even for children with Down syndrome. “He was reported to have become very fussy with his intake and his diet was said to contain no fruit or vegetables at that time,” the paediatrician said. “He had only gained 300 grams in the last 11 months.” Connor was prescribed multivitamins.

Advertisement

However, during his final admission, doctors found the multivitamin the family was using, known in the findings only as “the Product”, did not contain vitamin C. “I am concerned that a product such as [the one Connor was taking] is available in Australia. I believe that it is misleading to call this product a multivitamin when it misses essential vitamins such as vitamin C,” the pediatrician said. “It is my clinical opinion that Connor would not have had vitamin C deficiency, and the clinical features of scurvy that led to his death, if he had been taking a different multivitamin that contained vitamin C.” The multivitamin’s manufacturer offered “sincere condolences” but rejected the paediatrician’s criticism and said there was “no basis on which to draw the conclusion that [its multivitamin] has contributed to Connor’s death”. The coroner agreed there was not enough evidence to say the multivitamin caused or contributed to the death.

Advertisement

Instead, she focused on the failure to detect Connor’s severe vitamin C deficiency in time. AAP

title: The political foes chasing down KPMG’s ‘wolves’ have not finished yet
text:
Advertisement

BusinessCompaniesBig four consultants The political foes chasing down KPMG’s ‘wolves’ have not finished yet Colin Kruger Updated September 3, 2026 — 12:43pm ,first published September 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Labor senator Deborah O’Neill sent a shockwave across the country with her bombshell revelations of the conduct at accounting/consulting giant KPMG – and it has even led some to call for her elevation to a higher office. “Deb should be a cabinet minister, in my view. And I’d say to the prime minister, happy to put it on public record, make this woman a cabinet minister because she’s formidable. She’s a force of nature. She’s got a very strong moral compass. She’s very thorough, and she’s very collegiate.” Paul Scarr, Barbara Pocock, Deborah O’Neill, Tania Lawrence and Scott Buchholz address the media at Parliament House after the June 19 public hearing. Getty Images This praise did not come from an anonymous factional source within the ALP jockeying for favour. It was the Liberal National Party Queensland senator Paul Scarr.

Advertisement

He was singing her praises, having shared the star chamber atmosphere of the public hearings that have forensically torn apart the leadership of the global consulting giant – and other groups associated the scandal such as law firms and the accounting peak body – with ferocity, humour and a tight-knit kinship among political rivals. Related Article Consulting Macquarie director met ex-KPMG colleagues amid $700m audit bid The common cause of exposing the corporate wrongdoing is in sharp contrast to the growing political divide in Canberra as One Nation’s ascendancy – it is the one party not represented on the committee – upsets the traditional political order. At the June hearings, O’Neill, the committee chair, praised her colleagues, including Scarr, Greens senator Barbara Pocock, deputy chair and Liberal National Party MP Scott Buchholz, Liberal senator Dave Sharma and Labor senator Tania Lawrence. “I am so pleased to be sitting here with my colleagues today and undertake this work in the national interest,” she said at the June hearings.

Advertisement

The last two words are a point that O’Neill emphasises when it comes to what makes this committee click. “We share a view of what our role is as parliamentarians and what voters expect us to do, in their interests,” she says in an interview. Related Article Opinion

Whistleblowers The dismantling of KPMG is about to begin Colin Kruger Senior business reporter “I think it restores hope in the democratic project that people are able to see us working together for them as parliamentarians.” The parliamentary hearings have uncovered cases of ethical breaches by some KPMG executives, and it would appear these occurred in the pursuit of profit. In contrast, the public interest is the only upside for many of the politicians on the committee, despite the incredible capabilities and work ethic on display.

Advertisement

O’Neill was forced to fight for her job in 2021 in an internal factional tussle with Kristina Keneally for top spot on Labor’s Senate ticket. Scarr, a Liberal moderate, seems unlikely to find favour in a climate where One Nation poses an existential threat. Pocock, who was elected to the Senate in 2022, says her focus remains on housing, holding KPMG to account and the environment ahead of her term expiring at the next federal election. Both Scarr and Pocock say there is a shared outrage uniting the committee across the political trenches. “It is a shared mission, and I think it’s shared values, which is: ‘Hold these bastards to account for their greed and their moral failures,’ ” Pocock tells this masthead.

Advertisement

Both also allude to a shared purpose on the outcome that is needed. “I think the committee also knows there’s a moment here – that we don’t want to lose this moment. We don’t want to lose this opportunity for reform to occur,” Scarr says. “There we are in the parliament chasing down these wolves … we are not the regulator … we should have a regulatory system that actually imposes very painful, large penalties for such unmitigated greed,” Pocock says. Senator Deborah O’Neill, who brought the scandal to light in March, questions KPMG executives at a hearing on June 19. Getty Part of what is feeding the committee’s outrage is that O’Neill, Scarr and Pocock were uncovering appalling behaviour at rival PwC – relating to its tax leaks scandal – at the same time as senior KPMG executives were engaging in their own misdeeds and then allegedly trying to cover it up.

Advertisement

Pocock acknowledges the crucial role played by Liberal senator Richard Colbeck in the PwC hearings, which were winding up in 2024 when the KPMG whistleblower complained to his bosses of appalling behaviour by some of the firm’s most senior partners – including auditors accessing confidential client data to win new business. This includes confidential Lendlease board documents about rival tenders for its audit contract. It is a massive breach of trust for the auditors who require unfettered access to customer information to assess and certify the credibility of their financial accounts – a service that is essential to the integrity of financial markets. It explains some of the outrage at KPMG’s mistreatment of the whistleblower, including a covert search of his work laptop. Loading

Advertisement

“The search which occurred early in the day on 30 May [2024], I think, with my best recollection, was authorised by me and was in the context of us being concerned that the individual might be seeking other employment. We were concerned about whether information from KPMG might have been shared outside of the organisation,” KPMG’s former audit head Julian McPherson told the committee at its June hearing. O’Neill: “God forbid!” Lawrence: “The irony!” Scarr: “You were concerned about your own information, but not Lendlease’s!” O’Neill: “Sorry, colleagues. I know that there’s outrage here, but let’s just get everything on the record.”

Advertisement

Pocock: “It’s just gobsmacking!” In an interview, Sharma says the KPMG executives clearly knew what they were doing was wrong. “The thing that was probably more shocking is the degree to which people tried to cover this up through various means, so either you know by directly lying or not being candid and honest.” Both Scarr and Sharma represent the traditional party of big business, but say the issue of wrongdoing is what provides the unity with an unusual kindred spirit like the Greens. “As politicians, we all have an interest in holding institutions to account and looking out for the public interest. And often, those things are not really a matter of partisanship,” Sharma says. Loading

Advertisement

Another fiery exchange from the hearings concerned the use of the euphemism “falling short” by KPMG and accounting body CAANZ to repeatedly describe all sorts of illicit behaviour, which has now seen staff sacked and triggered multiple investigations. Scarr: “You use the phrase ‘fall short’ – ‘They have fallen short’ as if there’s some aspiration up here and you got to 90 per cent of it. Why? … Can I suggest to you that perhaps the better phrase would be ‘egregious breach’?” O’Neill: “Failure.” Scarr: “Would you accept that?” The fact that the committee includes so many who have life experience outside politics has really helped, Scarr says. His previous career included a long stint at Allens – one of the firms at the core of KPMG’s whistleblower actions.

Advertisement

Scarr also worked as general counsel and company secretary of ASX-listed PanAust Ltd. It involved working closely with its auditors and gave him a clear-eyed understanding of just how appalling the KPMG breaches were. Pocock had a career as an economist and academic before her political life began. “I think we are actually a fairly values-driven group of people,” Pocock says. “And while we are all party animals, I mean, you don’t get to be a Greens senator without your blood running green. And the same for Labor and Liberals – there are plenty of reasons why we are antagonistic to each other – but I do think ... we’ve all had quite a bit of life experience,” she says. Greens senator Barbara Pocock will not contest for another term at the 2028 election. Alex Ellinghausen

Advertisement

Scarr says each has had an important role to play, but singled out O’Neill, who spent decades working as a high school teacher before her political career. “Obviously, there’s Deb’s strong moral compass, which I like to think we all have. But also you know I’ve got the legal background, the professional services background, so I understand how that world works. And Barbara’s very forensic. Barbara will be a loss to the Senate,” he says of Pocock’s recently announced plans to retire at the 2028 election. “I think Deb’s leadership has been strong and courageous, and Paul Scarr’s also,” Pocock says. “There are plenty of Greens colleagues who think I was nuts for saying that. It’s not the way that Parliament always works. It thrives, and the media thrive, on conflict,” she admits. Senator Paul Scarr at the June hearings in Canberra. Getty Images

Advertisement

Pocock says the big test for this unusual political unity will come when the government is forced to enact an effective solution to these crucial firms being overrun by greed and bad behaviour, and whistleblower reforms, a challenge it largely failed after the PwC scandal. Related Article Consulting An email, a smiling emoji and the expulsion of a KPMG high-flyer “I think the real test for the differences between us will come … and that is, what happens? Will Labor have the courage to reform the governance of these organisations with proper directors and proper responsibilities for a board, and really significant penalties and proper structural reform of a failed partnership model?” The behind-the-scenes industry response will be formidable – not just from KPMG, which has conceded as little as it can in the brutal hearings so far. Pocock is under no illusions about what the big firms really think of her and O’Neill. The feedback from insiders at these firms has provided a clear picture.

Advertisement

“[We get] feedback from people from inside the Big Four who say there are certainly figures within the leadership of the Big Four who say, of Deb and I, ‘Oh those two women, what would they know? We just wait for their caravan to move on. They are just a couple of amateurs on our very complex terrain.’ ” It will be front of mind on Friday as the committee grills the corporate regulator ASIC, and other parties that have yet to be announced. title: Developer Bathla told to fix defects as it teeters on the edge of liquidation
text:
Advertisement

The state’s building regulator has ordered the collapsed Sydney developer Bathla Group to fix serious defects in one of its major projects as administrators desperately work to save the company from liquidation. With the deadline to save the developer nearing its end, Bathla’s main corporate entity Universal Property Group has been hit with a prohibition and building work rectification order for its under-construction development in the Illawarra’s Kembla Grange, preventing any buyer from living there until the defects are fixed. Sue Mancuso and daughter Marie Sinclair stand in front of the fenced-off Kembla Grange development. Wolter Peeters Building Commission NSW identified 12 serious defects in the five-building development, including non-compliant installation of a waterproofing system at the basement slab. “The non-compliant waterproofing system to the basement slab soffit will lead to water ingress and cause unhealthy or dangerous conditions, loss of amenity for occupants and undue dampness or deterioration of building elements,” the order read.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Bathla collapse Why Bathla’s demise could help make apartment building in western Sydney more affordable Failure to comply with the requirements listed in the building work rectification order, which must be complied with within eight months, is a criminal offence. A prohibition order means an occupation certificate cannot be issued for the development until the building work rectification order is revoked by the commission. Marie Sinclair’s elderly parents are among buyers who purchased an apartment in the development, which they were told would be completed by December 2025. When she visited in September last year, she found doors with keys left unattended, graffitied walls, half-finished copper piping and multiple broken surfaces. Sinclair said after the building order was issued on Thursday “it is really good news” but she remained uncertain about the next steps.

Advertisement

“Does that mean they have eight months to have the rectifications completed? Also will purchasers need to wait eight more months before moving in?” Sinclair said. “For many of us, this means more money and rent and storage fees for everyone.” Bathla entered into voluntary administration last week with $3.3 billion in debts. For the past few days, administrators Teneo have been desperately trying to secure funding from private lenders to pay the company’s 350 staff by Thursday and finish its 45 construction projects. Teneo has been contacted for comment. When this masthead asked Bathla last month about the development, the company’s spokesperson said 80 per cent of the 108 units had been sold off the plan and that buyers would be able to move in “during October or November”. “On completion, the project will be handed to the buyers in great condition,” the spokesperson said at the time.

Advertisement

The NSW government on Thursday doubled down on its stance not to bail out Bathla, with Deputy Premier Prue Car saying they have to be very careful with taxpayers’ money. “We’re not going to be spending money that belongs to the people of NSW to bail out private creditors for a developer that has gone into administration or receivership,” she said. “We are interested in what we can do for subcontractors and for home owners or potential home owners, but we’re just not going to bail [Bathla] out because if we were to do that, the money would go to private creditors. “We’re just not going to do that. What about the workers who are owed millions in wages? What happens to that?” With Max Maddison

Sacked KPMG executive Eileen Hoggett is suing the firm after her abrupt dismissal over confidential client documents kept in her work locker. The NSW Supreme Court confirmed that a summons has been lodged in her name against a KPMG entity with the first hearing scheduled for September 23. Former chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett was expelled from KPMG in July. AAP No court documents are available at this stage. The court listing shows she is legally represented by employment law specialist Bryan Belling.

Advertisement

Related Article Big four consultants The political foes chasing down KPMG’s ‘wolves’ have not finished yet Hoggett, a former chief operating officer, has said previously that she copped a hefty financial penalty from being expelled from the firm in July. KPMG has been thrown into turmoil by damaging allegations aired by a whistleblower that confidential client data was accessed and used to win new clients. She was expelled from the firm in July after new evidence emerged to support a whistleblower’s allegation that sensitive Lendlease board documents had been kept in a locker in KPMG’s Sydney office. The board documents were used to win business with other clients. The locker was Hoggett’s. New CEO John Sams sacked her immediately over the issue, after Hoggett had previously denied the documents were in the locker.

Advertisement

“To say I am angry about this is an understatement. The conduct was totally unacceptable, and it is unacceptable that it has taken so long for us to get to this point,” Sams told partners when Hoggett’s expulsion was announced. “I was provided with a copy of an email dated back from 1 May 2023, three weeks ago, that would convey that I had a copy of Lendlease documents that were in my locker,” Hoggett told a public hearing into the whistleblower scandal last month. The email was tabled in the public hearing last month: “I think we confidentially allow him to look at the printed version in my locker when he is back in Sydney. He needs to do it sensitively without letting too many people know,” she said in an email that concluded with a smiley emoji. Hoggett told the hearing: “There is no one more disappointed in me than myself at this email,” but Hoggett also said she was still trying to ascertain the reason for her unprecedented sacking, and attested to the financial cost.

Advertisement

“I don’t get my accrued annual leave. I don’t get the retirement payment, which I contributed to as a partner for 21 years, and I did not get paid for the last month up until to the date of my expulsion. So [it’s a] significant financial penalty,” she said. Related Article Consulting The whistle that blew away KPMG’s aura as the guardians of financial credibility Hoggett had already resigned over the scandal but had yet to leave the firm. She would have left with a significant retirement benefit – expected to exceed a million dollars – if that had proceeded. Former KPMG boss Andrew Yates, who resigned over the scandal in May, received a retirement payment of $2.4 million, including $1.7 million in lieu of notice. Hoggett told the hearing that her abrupt sacking had no precedent within the KPMG partnership, and she had no opportunity to respond.

Advertisement

“I was out walking one morning, and I received a call from the CEO [John Sams], who advised that I was being expelled. I asked to understand the rationale and the reason for that because that is unprecedented. It’s something that’s never occurred in our partnership before.” Law firm Corrs, who is advising Hoggett in relation to the regulatory investigations by ASIC and accounting body CAANZ, declined to comment. KPMG was approached for comment. At a public hearing of the parliamentary committee on Friday, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) is expected to provide an update on the investigation. title: ‘Did you regularly lie?’: Charles Perrottet admits he fibbed to friends

Follow the ICAC hearing live Right-wing Liberal operative Charles Perrottet has told a corruption inquiry he wanted to grow the conservative faction in the Hills area of Sydney, but insisted he did not use money from disgraced developer Jean Nassif to achieve political outcomes. Perrottet on Thursday returned to the Independent Commission Against Corruption, which is investigating whether he was one of three Liberal apparatchiks who shared in a $2 million bribe from Nassif. Jean Nassif and Charles Perrottet. Developers have long been banned from making political donations in NSW.

Counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, suggested to Perrottet the reason he attended a lunch at the Chiswick home of Nassif in September 2020 was to celebrate a significant payment from the developer days earlier. The commission has previously heard a $148,500 cheque was paid to Beckington, the lobby firm run by his Liberal allies Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis, on September 11. Loading Greenwood and Ellis also allegedly shared in the $2 million bribe from Nassif.
